#1463. Boston was a lovely holiday romance, but let's leave it there. Talk of taking Tartan Army back there every two years is just cringeworthy

Published: 11:18 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 13:03 EST, 13 November 2026

Boston was the loveliest little holiday romance. An unforgettable moment in time. But let’s just leave it at that, shall we?

Can’t we just allow those involved in the shenanigans around the World Cup last summer to reflect misty-eyed on doorways to Xanadu being opened by the tilt of the kilt and maybe even the heady nights they can’t remember much about at all?

Or does everything have to be milked to the max these days? Flogged like a dead horse to benefit someone or other. Ruined, really. Played out until every scintilla of fun has been drained out of it.

A bit like Yes, Sir, I Can Boogie. That started out as a bona-fide hoot. A half-cut Andy Considine dressing up in drag with his friends and family during his stag do in London in 2015 and making a music video around Baccara’s 1977 hit. It went viral. Obviously. It was – and is – hilarious.

When Scotland’s players resurrected it in the dressing room in Serbia five years later – with Considine as part of the squad – after the national team had ended a 23-year wait to make it to a major competition, it was simply inspired.

Every second of those infectious scenes exuded elation, joy, togetherness and pin-sharp humour, a killer recipe for the interludes that make life and living so great.

Now? Even the opening bars of the song bring on a sense of dread. It was splattered over T-shirts, played everywhere on repeat and still gets aired at every Scotland home game.

The Tartan Army march to Boston's Fenway Park baseball stadium

It’s boring. It’s been done to death and now lives firmly in that grim, stagnant swamp known as Scottish mainstream culture along with munchy boxes, Bitz N Pieces, theatre shows about the Old Firm and ex-footballers suddenly developing a personality and getting involved in stage shows to tell the world how Wee Dazza once did Big Jazza a beauty in the dressing-room by leaving a squelchy banana in his shoe. The banter anawrat.

Everything ends up spoiled here and it looks like we’re already well down that road with the Tartan Army thanks to the news breaking that the Scottish FA are in talks with the State of Massachusetts over a biennial friendly match at the Gillette Stadium, the black hole amid the festivity at the finals thanks to struggling past Haiti and embarrassing ourselves against Morocco.

State senator Paul Feeney has been across the pond to press the flesh. Massachusetts senate president Karen Spilka is already talking about staging Tartan Day – presumably some rip-off of that twee, shortbread-tin abomination in New York – and ‘other events’.

The heart sinks. Listen, the minute politicians get involved in any kind of ‘happening’, the best thing to do is give it a wide berth.

Mind you, before the Big Swerve, it might be worthwhile having someone remind these characters from The Bay State that Massachusetts’ first contribution to Scotland supporters hitting town in summer involved hiking the cost of the 25-mile train ride from Boston to the ground from $20 to a ludicrous $80.

What unfolded there in mid-June was nothing to do with them. It was everything to do with spontaneity. As it ought to be. A glorious coming-together of all sorts of folk up for a right, royal carry-on.

There were so many glorious vignettes. Scotland punters taking over Red Sox games. Bars running out of beer. Mass marches. Local women, doped-up on Outlander, telling TikTok how a bunch of jakeys intent on drinking anything within arm’s reach – except Bud Light, of course – were making them feel ‘seen’.

The Tartan Army make their presence known in Boston during the summer's World Cup

It was brilliant. A short spell in which stars aligned and magic happened. Boston had everything the Tartan Army required. And going by the testimony of Bostonians, the Tartan Army brought badly needed vitality back to the streets of a city quietened by Covid and other factors.

Everybody won. Everyone there still dines out on the memory. But that’s where it should stay. In the memory. These conversations about trying to recapture that spirit, recreate it every two years around some meaningless friendly against opposition unconfirmed and possible business meetings on the periphery, feel quite sad. How can it have any legs long-term?

Joe and Josephine Punter have moved on. They’re on the batter in other places now. Next week, it’s Switzerland for a Nations League game. After that, it’s wherever the draw for the Euro qualifiers throws them. New cities. New adventures. As football away days ought to be. In, out, shake it all about.

Away days are not about teaming up with suit-wearing dignitaries to be paraded at the town hall, like performing seals in plaid – even though there does appear to be an element of the Scotland support that enjoys that kind of thing.

Away days are not about being used as political capital or forming part of some constructed ‘festival’.

Look, in most aspects of life, it’s generally best not to go back. Sticking traffic cones on top of statues all over town won’t be as funny next time. There won’t be a 20,000-strong travelling support spending their life savings on games an entire generation had been waiting for. There won’t be anything like the same buzz, if any.

Some folk might fancy returning once, just to see if it feels the same. The idea that this is going to be a big deal every two years, though, feels deeply misguided.

Boston’s Irish. Not Scottish. That Tartan Week nonsense in New York is a toe-curlingly awful melange of kilts, Scottie dogs and actors living in America telling everyone back home how to vote.

No self-respecting Scot should give it house room. If there is a plan for the same thing in Boston, the same rules apply.

Like NYC, it’ll suit those from the political class in the mood for a junket, of course. John Swinney will already be counting the air miles if there’s another game in Massachusetts to go to.

The public, of course, is still counting the cost of the First Minister’s last trip there for the World Cup. The bill came in at £45,000 for him and two senior aides to fly business class. The entire trip for government staff came to more than £98,000.

Swinney plays the role with aplomb at these affairs, supping a pint in his Scotland top. The Scottish Football Association need to ask themselves this, though: why should they put themselves at the heart of some kind of cock-eyed project to build bridges politically?

The Tartan Army leave their signature traffic cone in a park in Boston

First up, the players are hardly likely to welcome a pointless week in America being added to a jam-packed schedule. More importantly, though, what exactly has this SNP-led administration, outwith giving a few bob to grassroots, done for Scottish football down the years?

From this vantage point, they’ve been no friend to the national game or its followers. The Offensive Behaviour at Football Act, repealed in 2018, was a scandalous piece of legislation that criminalised fans and made going to football unpleasant.

Clubs have had to fight tooth and nail to secure trials to sell pints inside stadiums when other sports are allowed to do what they like. After trouble in Glasgow city centre ahead of the Old Firm League Cup final two years ago, Swinney stated that ‘the clubs have got a responsibility to make sure their fans behave properly’.

Inside their grounds, yes. What are they meant to do, though, about teenagers running amok on Argyle Street?

Looking after that is the job of the police. Of course, anyone reading 1919 magazine, funded by the Scottish Police Federation, earlier this year will have noted an article about policing around football being ‘chaotic’ and understaffed because of SNP Government budget cuts.

Just like everything else in this sorry little nation built on buying votes for ‘free stuff’, Police Scotland is creaking at the seams. Why would anyone want to get involved in another transatlantic piece of theatre selling some false, outdated, vaguely comical vision of it to foreigners?

A pointless Scotland friendly – served up as part of some forced, hackneyed ‘cultural exchange’ or not – is hardly an idea to be getting on board with.

Pure dead brilliant, it won’t be. More like pure cringe.

#1462. Former England star Dele Alli in line for huge £8.3m payday after selling his image rights company

Published: 10:30 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 13:07 EST, 13 November 2026

Former Tottenham star Dele Alli is set for a mammoth £8.3million payday as he plans to close down his image rights company, Dele Alli Promotions.

The now 30-year-old may be without a club but was not so foolish as to not prepare for life without a bumper contract, with his company boasting the sizeable sum in assets.

However, Alli will have to hand over £685,362 to the tax man - but this is a drop in the ocean in relation to the eyewatering £7.6million he is set to receive.

The former England international has been without a club for over 19 months, having last been in action for Cesc Fabregas' Como side in Serie A but only played one game, coming on as an 81st minute sub against AC Milan and receiving a red card just nine minutes later.

But Alli has several projects alongside Dele Alli Promotions keeping him busy while he is attempting to get back to full fitness and find a new club.

He owns and manages a private residential real estate holding company named Future Homes Investments, which owns and rents six properties worth more than £1.5million.

Dele Alli is looking at a very healthy payday after closing down his image rights company

The Englishman has played just ten minutes of professional football since February 2023

The Former Spurs man was forced to wear an Arsenal shirt on his Instagram story after losing a game of EAFC 27 to a fellow streamer

And his smallest company, Dele Investments still holds £336,267 in assets.

Most recently the former English international has branched out into livestreaming on Twitch with a skateboard, an array of expensive designer bags, and at least 48 pairs of shoes providing his backdrop.

He has already picked up traction on his channel by calling up old teammates such as Harry Kane, Eric Dier and Jack Grealish while live.

And while playing EAFC 27 with other steamers such as IShowSpeed, who recently forced Alli to wear an Arsenal shirt on Instagram after losing a wager to the 21-year-old American.

It is a far cry from his heady days as a player, when Dele twice picked up the PFA Young Player of the Year award and starred for England on their way to the semi-finals of the 2018 World Cup.

During an interview in 2023 on The Overlap, he opened up about his harrowing past, having to smoke and sell drugs as young as seven years old and being hung over a bridge by a man from neighbouring estate when he was just 11.

This resulted in the midfielder turning to sleeping pills and alcohol to suppress his feelings and help him through his trauma.

#1461. New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Researchers tagged dozens of proteins that can cross the blood-brain barrier and are important for brain health.Credit: K. H. Fung/SPL

For decades, scientists thought of the blood–brain barrier as an impenetrable layer. Over time that view has changed, as researchers realized the barrier was more permeable than first thought. Now, a team have catalogued almost 100 proteins that can pass through it to maintain brain health1.

The team also found that the transport of some of these crucial proteins breaks down in mice with brain diseases that mimic early-stage Alzheimer’s disease.

“The paradigm in the field has been that the blood–brain barrier is normally impermeable and then becomes leaky as a result of Alzheimer’s disease,” says study co-author Andrew Yang, a neuroscientist at Gladstone Institute of Neurological Disease in San Francisco, California. Instead, his team’s work suggests that the blood–brain barrier actively imports proteins that the brain needs to function and the loss of these proteins drives the dysfunction seen early in the disease, he adds.

Yang and his colleagues developed a technique to label a large array of proteins in the blood and track those that can enter the brain. Of the 861 proteins they mapped, 92 crossed the blood–brain barrier into the brain. Most of these proteins were produced in distant organs, particularly the liver.

The team focused on apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1), which has been linked to potential protective effects against Alzheimer’s disease2. Once inside the brain, APOA1 stimulates brain cells called astrocytes to release cholesterol, which is important for maintaining the synapses through which neurons communicate. But how the protein crossed the blood–brain barrier has been unclear until now, says Yang.

His team found that two receptors for APOA1 — SR-B1 and ABCA1 — are present on the blood–brain barrier as well as astrocytes. This suggests how the protein moves from the blood–brain barrier to the specific brain cells that need them, the authors say.

When Yang’s team blocked the ABCA1 receptor in laboratory-grown astrocytes, the protein no longer had the same cholesterol-regulating effects.

Scientists have long known that the blood–brain barrier breaks down as Alzheimer’s advances, letting harmful molecules leak into the brain. Yang’s team found that a different problem emerges first.

Using their labelling technique in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease, the researchers found that the blood–brain barrier stopped importing protective proteins such as APOA1 into the brain before the barrier began to break down. This disruption to the protein transport was accompanied by a loss of neuronal connections, behavioural changes and other early hallmarks of the disease.

Yang and the team wondered whether increasing the supply of APOA1 in the blood might help to counter some of the damage caused by Alzheimer’s disease. To find out, the team engineered mice with Alzheimer’s to produce extra APOA1 in the liver. When more APOA1 crossed the blood–brain barrier and entered the brain, the mice showed fewer Alzheimer’s-disease-related markers. For example, they had reduced fat build-up in astrocytes and lower levels of inflammatory molecules.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03655-2

Zhou, H. et al. Cell https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.039 (2026).

#1460. My Everton #179: Loyalty & Love From Namibia

My love for Everton began when I was just eight years old.

At that age, football was more than just a game to me; it was something that brought me happiness, excitement and dreams.

Wayne Rooney was my favourite player and my biggest inspiration. He was not just a footballer I admired; he was someone I looked up to. In fact, when we played football in my village, my friends would call me "Rooney" because of how much I admired him and wanted to play like him.

When Rooney eventually moved to Manchester United, I found myself facing a difficult decision. Naturally, I wanted to follow him because he was my role model.

I thought about becoming a Manchester United supporter, but something inside me would not allow it. No matter how much I admired Rooney, my heart still belonged to Everton.

I realised my connection with the Club was much deeper than supporting a single player. It was a love that had already taken root in my heart.

Then came another special moment in my Everton journey. When Jordan Pickford joined the club in 2017, I was also transitioning into playing as a goalkeeper.

Watching him defend the goal inspired me in a new way. I saw in him someone I could learn from, someone who motivated me to become a better goalkeeper and strengthened my love for Everton.

From that moment, I became even more certain that Everton was my club, and I was proud to call myself a true Evertonian.

Being an Everton supporter in Namibia is not always easy.

We are few, and sometimes it feels like we are a rare breed. As far as I know, I have only met two other Everton supporters here, including my girlfriend, who is also an Evertonian.

Most of my friends often ask: "Bro, why do you support Everton?"

But my answer has always been simple: I support Everton because my love for this club is all about loyalty, passion, and the memories that have shaped who I am.

For me, Everton is more than just a football club. It is part of my childhood, part of my identity, and part of my story. From an eight-year-old boy who admired Wayne Rooney to the young man I am today, my love for this club has remained unchanged.

Every match, every goal, every victory, and even every heartbreak has added another chapter to my journey as an Evertonian.

I may be thousands of kilometres away, but my heart has always been with Everton.

Geography cannot weaken a love that has lasted for more than a decade, and difficult seasons cannot erase the memories that made me fall in love with this beautiful club.

I was there in the good times, I've been here in the difficult times and I will be here when the glory returns. Because once Everton gets into your heart, it never truly leaves.

My Everton shares first-hand accounts describing the most-treasured memories of fans, players, and staff both past and present.

#1458. Egypt sack their manager for 'negative impact on team image' after he fainted when fight broke out between his TWO wives with punches and hair-pulling in a bar

Published: 13:16 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 13:48 EST, 13 November 2026

Egypt will begin their African Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying matches with a new manager after their previous head coach was sacked amid a torrid breakdown of both of his marriages.

Hossam Hassan was handed his marching orders on Saturday after an incident in August which saw his two wives embroiled in a vicious fight, captured and shared on social media.

Hassan's first wife Howaida El-Gharbawy and his second Dina 'Dan Adam' Mustafa started the argument while at a hotel bar in the upscale Porto Marina resort on Egypt's north coast.

El-Gharbawy and Mustafa were videoed arguing with Hassan in the middle attempting to cool tensions, but the duo came to blows, with punches thrown and hair pulled as screams filled the air.

Such was the stress of the incident that Hassan is believed to have fainted as he tried to separate the two women.

Horrified public onlookers watched as the physical fight grew with relatives of the trio getting involved, and security was called before Hassan was taken to hospital.

En Égypte, un violent différend a éclaté entre... les deux femmes du sélectionneur égyptien, Hossam Hassan. 🇪🇬😳Le conflit a dégénéré en échauffourée avec coups et tirage de cheveux, avant que des jeunes et des passages n'interviennent dans la bagarre. pic.twitter.com/pvRUSMtAsD

Egypt head coach Hossam Hassan was sacked this week after a fight broke out between his two wives

Hassan's first wife Howaida El-Gharbawy and his second Dina 'Dan Adam' Mustafa started the argument while at a hotel in the upscale Porto Marina resort

The 60-year-old is believed to have fainted while trying to separate the two women

Both women are believed to have been left with cuts and bruises following the vicious scrap, while Hassan, despite briefly losing consciousness, was left unharmed.

His lawyers later told Sky News Arabia, via the Sun, that he was not suffering a health crisis during the incident, and that he remained in good health.

But in the days that followed, Hassan started proceedings to divorce El-Gharbawy, who he has been married to for decades. The couple also share three children.

The 60-year-old has a further two children with second wife Mustafa, who Le Parisien alleges also filed for divorce in the days after the footage went viral on social media.

The Egyptian Football Association ensured that Hassan's professional life took a similar nosedive, sharing in a statement that his dismissal was due in part to reputational damage the scandal might be doing to the national team.

'After analysing all the circumstances and events of the past few days, as well as their consequences and the negative impact they have had on the positive image and stability of our national team, the Board of Directors has decided, within the framework of its responsibilities, to dismiss coach Hossam Hassan and his entire technical staff and to end his tenure,' their statement read.

Mustafa's lawyer Mohamed Shams gave an interview on Sky News Arabia claiming that his client had been the victim of a 'premeditated attack'.

'We hoped it wouldn't come to divorce, but things escalated to this level.'

Hassan married his second wife in 2015, with Egyptian law allowing Muslim men to marry up to four women, providing that any wives have been formally informed that another marriage is to take place.

The law mandates that the husband is also obligated to treat all of his wives equally with regard to housing, financial support and standard of living.

Hassan had been married to his first wife El-Gharbawy for decades, with the pair sharing three of his five children

Hassan and Mustafa briefly separated four years ago before recoupling before the spat that ended both of his marriages.

As well as being relieved of his duties, Hassan was also sanctioned by the Supreme Council for Media Regulation, leaving him unable to publicly address the media following his sacking.

Mohamed Salah and Co will now play their first qualifier of the international break against Malawi under new head coach Ali Maher.

The former Liverpool star could be among those Pharaohs stars privately pleased with the departure of Hassan, after he was benched by his ex-manager for the last two international clashes.

When asked why the superstar and national team captain had been left on the sidelines for the ties, Hassan had said: 'It is not right for a country of 120 million people for the national team to depend on one player.'

#1457. Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool

Andoni Iraola spun on his heels, turned his back to the action and began to bite his nails. Managers often envisage the worst outcome when the clock ticks down, and here, in the 93rd minute, Bournemouth had a corner.

He needn’t have worried. As the set-piece was swung in, Alisson Becker moved powerfully off his line and plucked the ball from the air, a catch that essentially confirmed Liverpool would leave Dorset with three points. It was a catch, too, that put the gloss on another impeccable personal afternoon.

When Iraola took charge at Anfield, one question he had to answer – given Bournemouth had conceded 167 goals in his three years in charge – was whether he could make Liverpool defensively resilient. This dour 1-0 success, though, proves he is taking them in the right direction: he is the first Liverpool manager since Joe Fagan in 1983 to start with five unbeaten league games.

Alexander Isak might have scored the goal that leaves Bournemouth winless in the Premier League but this success owed everything to Alisson’s enduring brilliance – a comment that also applies to Virgil van Dijk – the enormous promise of Jérémy Jacquet and the grit of Ronaldo Araújo.

You go to top level football matches hoping to see something that will take your breath away and how Alisson did that in the 17th minute with a reflex save from an Evanilson backheel, the shape of his body resembling a fielder in the slips diving to prevent a boundary.

It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”

Don’t confuse positivity about one aspect of the team as being a guide to its collective health. There was always a chance this contest would become a cagey affair and, Evanilson’s chance aside, the opening 45 minutes were as flat as you could imagine.

Iraola again played his three £100m+ signings but Bradley Barcola is still adjusting to the physicality of English football and Florian Wirtz is still finding it difficult to impose himself on a game; patience with the German will not be infinite.

He would do worse than to look at Isak, who is now on a run of four goals in four league games and is influencing games in the manner Liverpool envisaged when they broke the British transfer record to sign him last August.

Isak had an unusual afternoon. His only shot in the first half almost took out some low-flying pigeons, a cross early in the second half was sliced so badly that the weekend hackers on the nearby Queens Park golf course would have felt a flood of sympathy but then he got his third opening.

Cody Gakpo, who could have been in Manchester City blue had the cards played out differently earlier this month, wriggled down the right flank and squeezed in a cross that Isak seized upon and turned in from six yards. Liverpool never looked back.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

“A striker’s job is like this,” Iraola said, who badgered Isak persistently to press Bournemouth’s defence. “He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control. He has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition’s half and have more meaningful possession. And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goals.”

One, ultimately, was enough to see off Bournemouth, whose start to the campaign is something of a riddle. They shouldn’t be anywhere near the relegation places but that is the reality and Thursday’s historic Europa League win in Real Sociedad couldn’t mask the home crowd’s frustration.

“Our attitude and effort is good,” head coach Marco Rose said. “But, at this level, small things and little details decide games.”

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola said: “I’m obviously happy with the result because I know this is a difficult place to come, very difficult place to get three points. And we could see it, especially in the beginning of the game. In the first 20 minutes we weren’t at the level [required] and it cost us. We finished the first half better and in the second half we played better, but that beginning of the game has surprised us, not surprised us [because] we knew where we were coming but it [was] difficult for us.”

Jeremy Jacquet has made the kind of quietly authoritative start to his Liverpool career that showed why there was such excitement in February within the club when they completed his deal. So much focus on so many players but Jacquet has never been anything other 7.5/8 out of 10.

"Let's go! One of many!" Virgil van Dijk giving Jérémy Jacquet his POTM award after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth ⭐️ pic.twitter.com/6xWvjmrF8Y

"That's a big moment to me to play with Virgil!" 🫡Jérémy Jacquet after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth! pic.twitter.com/UsTimGME39

Cody Gakpo has been Liverpool’s stand-out forward this term and he was at the heart of Isak’s goal this afternoon. Speaking about the job the Dutchman is doing to fill the void left by Mohamed Salah on the right flank, Ashley Young said on Sky Sports: “Players have to step up when you lose big players and you get the opportunities. I think Cody Gakpo is doing that. He’s a bit fortunate [in the build-up to Liverpool’s goal] but you create your own luck. He gets the ball down the line, that’s what you want to do and he puts the ball in the box. That’s what Isak’s waiting for.”

Fair play to anyone who retained Brobbey in their Fantasy Football teams this week...

4 - Brian Brobbey is the fourth player in Premier League history to score a hat-trick against the side starting the day top of the table, after Robbie Fowler v Aston Villa in November 1998, Dirk Kuyt v Man Utd in March 2011, and Romelu Lukaku v Man Utd in May 2013.Unstoppable. pic.twitter.com/vygVYazIQD

Maresca’s side maintain their immaculate record, but boy were they made to work for it this afternoon.

Sunderland are still 5-3 down but have not given up the ghost. Surely the best match of the season so far?

It ends goalless at Elland Road after Mitchell’s goal was disallowed for offside. Kamada went close to breaking the deadlock in the final stages...

Daichi Kamada can't guide his header on target! ❌ pic.twitter.com/AgKM6Q9apq

Bournemouth lose at the Vitality for the first time in 13 matches as Iraola makes a winning return to the South Coast. Liverpool were hardly impressive, but to their credit they managed the final stages of this match with a minimum of fuss.

Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium with a win! ✅ pic.twitter.com/FSgvE6EGFB

Bournemouth are awarded a corner but Brooks’ delivery goes straight into the inviting gloves of Alisson.

Koumas pressures Petrovic, but the goalkeeper shows off some tidy footwork to escape the danger.

Bournemouth cannot get out though, and Petrovic is forced into a routine save off Koumas moments later.

Bournemouth win a free-kick in a dangerous position after a handball, but Scott cannot get his strike up and down fast enough and it sails over.

Araujo gets his pocket picked in the corner but Jebbison cannot compose himself and blasts his cross off the other side of the pitch.

Liverpool go the other way and win a corner, but Mac Allister puts too much air on his delivery and it is easily dealt with.

Rayan wins a free-kick as he holds off Kerkez on the halfway line. Bournemouth then switch play to the far side but Truffert’s speculative effort flies well over the bar.

Nyoni shows off his composure on the ball, playing simple passes on the half-turn to keep play flowing. The midfield area is quite congested, which suits Liverpool at this point in the game.

Liverpool are baiting Bournemouth’s press in an attempt to play around their front line. They are doing a good job at holding on to the ball and frustrating their opponents, for now.

Gravenberch and Koumas are on for Gakpo and Isak.

Brooks has brought some energy to Bournemouth’s forays down the left. He attempts to slip a ball into the left channel but Nyoni is wise to it and positions himself perfectly to cut it out.

Liverpool have dropped deep and Bournemouth wait patiently for an opening. They eventually find Tavernier in the left half-space but his cross flies over everyone.

That is his last contribution to the match as Rose rings the changes: Tavernier, Smith and Christie make way for Brooks, Jebbison and Cook.

Truffert spins in a teasing ball from the left but Jacquet does well to flick the ball away from the danger zone.

Truffert clears the resulting corner to safety.

Isak is concentrating his efforts in more central areas and here he almost gets played in behind but the ball just runs away from him. Better.

It’s raining goals in Manchester and no prizes for guessing who has scored for Sunderland. Brobbey has his hat-trick.

Brobbey has his hat-trick and the look on Enzo Maresca’s face as he assesses the defending from his team. They’ve been great pouring forward, less so trying to stymie Sunderand’s attack. But this is one of those games where you just sit back and enjoy the unfolding drama. It’s been so good from both teams.

Semenyo gets his second goal of the afternoon to extend the league leaders’ advantage.

Chance! Jacquet jumps and wins the ball well inside Bournemouth’s half and his intervention sends the ball into Isak’s path. The forward just drags his effort wide and turns out he was in an offside postion anyhow.

What an afternoon this is turning out to be. There have been more slices than on an erratic day on the local municipal golf course and Ronald Araujo is the latest to be afflicted by the condition. None of that will matter to Andoni Iraola, though, as Alexander Isak’s fourth goal in four Premier League games has given Liverpool a huge advantage. They haven’t played with fluency but the breakthrough was significant.

Isak opens the scoring at the Vitality, finally getting into the box and sweeping in from close range. So much credit has to go to Gakpo who tiptoes past two Bournemouth defenders by the touchline before spearing a cross infield, and while he may not be attributed with the assist owing to a touch off Wirtz, his delivery makes it all the way through to Isak who taps in.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

Adams has been superb as one of Bournemouth’s two midfield sentries. Kerkez looks to have been played into the left channel but the American swoops in and shields the ball out of play before staring down his Hungarian opponent.

The second has already settled into a holding pattern, with neither side creating much. Isak makes a run down the right hand side and, with players loaded in the box, he blasts the ball high into the sky and beyond his team-mates. That pretty much sums things up.

City are in front. Again. Semenyo this time, he fires the ball beyond Roefs having collected a loose ball int he box.

A relatively slick Liverpool move sees the ball worked out to Araujo on the right who has minded to bomb on with increasing frequency, and while he’s able to win a corner, Szoboszlai’s delivery is cleared with a minimum of fuss.

Iraola came into this game saying that his side held an advantage having played two days earlier than Bournemouth in midweek. You would never have guessed it from what we have witnessed here today.

And right on cue, a frustrated Isak attempts a specultative effort from range which sails high and wide.

Can’t hold a lead today City. Wow, Sunderland are level again in an instant and it’s that man Brobbey again. There’s a VAR check going on to check for offside

So, this is not a rush to make a sweeping criticism, it’s simply an observation. But Liverpool fans will be looking at Bradley Barcola and  waiting to see that first burst, that moment of electricity, that has showed why they bought him. It’s like you look for a touch, a pass, a moment of skill. He’s just had a shot saved but it all seems very tentative for him at the moment. And that is what he needs - a moment.

Jacquet does brilliantly to close down Christie as the Scot was stealing into the box and looking to pull the trigger.

Chances! Barcola forces Petrovic into an awkward-looking save, before follow-up efforts from Wirtz and Gakpo are charged down.

Mac Allister is fouled 25 yards out moments later and Szoboszlai gets another go. Here, he drags his effort just wide.

It’s all happening at the Etihad. Cherki restores City’s lead with his third Premier League goal of the season.

It’s a great finish from Cherki to put City back in front but it doesn’t happen if Ndiaye is quick to read Danso’s risky pass and win possession. Sharp as a button in that moment.

Rayan Cherki puts Manchester City back in front! 💫 pic.twitter.com/PP4MAV9kw3

A really poor piece of defending from Kerkez gives Bournemouth a free-kick out on the right. Tavernier spins in an inswinger but Van Dijk heads clear. Truffert launches another assault on Liverpool’s box off the second phase but Alisson is wise to it and gathers.

It appears that Liverpool are beginning to settle, they take the opportunity to circulate the ball in front of Bournemouth’s first line of pressure, waiting for the right moment to pounce. The final pass is poor, though, and Araujo through-pass goes all the way through to Petrovic. It was aimed at Isak ...I think.

Some signs of life from Liverpool, as they create a substantial overload down their left, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Barcola and Isak meeting on that flank. Barcola attempts a sprint into the channel off the shoulder of the ball-side centre-back but he is deemed offside. Looked close, but a bit better from Liverpool.

Araujo has the chance to launch a long throw into the box but Silva beats Van Dijk to the summit and Petrovic gathers the loose ball.

Scott then sprays a wonderful ball over to Rayan on the right but his cutback to Tavernier comes to nothing after the midfielder loses the ball. Liverpool then spring a counter of their own, but Bournemouth recover and charge down a hopeful Gakpo effort from the edge of the box.

Liverpool will not be pleased with their start to this match. They’ve struggled to string more than three passes together without ceding possession and Isak has cut an isolated figure up top.

First time that Bournemouth have gone through the gears and the move ends with Alisson Becker saving brilliantly from Evanilson. It’s a funny stadium, here, as it can be quiet then all of a sudden a tempest whips up and you can sense the mood changing. Liverpool are struggling for alacrity and Andoni Iraola is keeping an eye on Florian Wirtz, who is moving gingerly after taking a bang to his left foot.

Some start at the Etihad. You had to wonder if a big early missed chance from Nilson Angulo was going to haunt Sunderland with City taking the lead just a few minutes later through a quite sublime free-kick from Enzo Fernandez. But Sunderland have immediately hit back. Maresca will decry the defending but it’s brilliant from Enzo Le Fee, who surges forward and then splits Nunes and Dias with an inch perfect pass that Brobbey takes beautifully in his stride before finishing.

On Fernandez’s free-kick before then, he’d very much shaped as if he’s going to cross the ball from a free-kick on the right side of the penalty area. He’d clearly spotted an opening in the top right though and, while giving the firm impression to Roefs he was going to whip in a cross, he obviously had other ideas. The execution was immaculate but it was telling just how effectively he’d managed to deceive the Sunderland goalkeeper. It was world class

A slight mix-up sees Kerkez and Wirtz bump into each other by the touchline. The Germany international limps away and grimaces but should be fine to continue.

Chance! Alisson makes amends with a stunning save. Tavernier had hit the by-line and lasered a cross to Evanilson who, with the ball slightly behind him, improvised and flicked it toward the near post. Alisson gets down swiftly and turns behind for a corner which comes to nothing.

Jacquet gives away a needless foul on the near side but Scott’s delivery goes straight into Alisson’s hands. The Brazilian’s throw out is poor, though, and Scott darts into Liverpool’s box, just unable to pick out a team-mate.

Barcola is presented with green grass to run into, but just as he builds a head of steam Hill comes across in a flash and snuffs out the foray forward.

Woah, Brobbey responds immediately, stealing in between City defenders before slotting past Donnarumma.

Enzo Fernandez opens the scoring at the Etihad with a direct free-kick from out wide. Really poor from Roefs who was caught napping. That’s Fernandez’s first City goal.

Wirtz earns a free-kick just outside the D. Bournemouth feel aggrieved as there looked to have been an earlier foul on Scott and to make matters worse Szoboszlai is standing over the ball.

His effort leaves Petrovic rooted to the spot but the ball veers just wide of the mark.

Evanilson’s willingness to drop deep is asking questions of Liverpool’s centre-backs. Do they follow him and risk disrupting their backline coverage?

The hosts attempt to work a short corner routine but Truffert’s eventual through-ball is too strong and the ball rolls out for a Liverpool goal-kick.

This wouldn’t go down as a fixture you would circle for being noteworthy but make no mistake this is a huge afternoon for Liverpool. They have had some days at the Vitality Stadium in recent years and last season’s defeat put a huge dent in Arne Slot’s hopes of trying to find a revival. It’s also a big test for Bournemouth, coming down from the euphoria of beating Real Sociedad. Let’s see how it all transpires.

Evanilson makes a smart run into the right channel and while Jacquet gets his foot on the ball he’s instantly smothered by Scott and the ball goes out for a Liverpool goal-kick. A sign of how high both sides will be willing to jump in search of the ball.

Both sides will look to force mistakes out of the other and Szoboszlai is able to pick Adams’ pocket on the halfway line. He offloads to Araujo who runs into a cul de sac down the right flank.

We are under way at the Vitality. Bournemouth are in their customary black-and-red home shirts kicking from right to left and Liverpool are in their white away kit and red shorts.

The players have emerged from the tunnel, Van Dijk and Smith at the front of the lines. A few pyrotechnics add to the atmosphere but one thing missing is the accidental sitting in the wrong dugout from the returning Iraola. He knows where he’s going.

Andoni Iraola returns to Bournemouth this weekend knowing what to expect from players he understands so well. Sadly, I do not mean Liverpool’s.

Having built his reputation creating a hard-working, well-drilled team rich in potential, Iraola is responsible for infusing those same characteristics into the most expensively assembled squad in Liverpool history.

His first six games demonstrate it is no quick fix. The Basque coach is the first Liverpool appointment to work with more than £700m of recent signings while being entitled to feel he has been dealt a bad hand.

Everything Iraola has said and done so far screams that he is searching for the right blend in his starting XI while having to eradicate negative traits, with and without the ball. It was telling that the excellent performance of his youngsters against Tottenham Hotspur in midweek offered the clearest hint of Iraola’s vision than anything we have seen with all the high-priced stars on the pitch.

There is a reason the Kop stood to acclaim the energy and application of youngsters Lewis Koumas, James McConnell and Trey Nyoni – and why Iraola keeps name-checking them. Iraola is indebted to them for issuing a reminder of the non-negotiables that come with being a Liverpool footballer; regardless of price tag and reputation, leaving everything on the pitch is compulsory. It is a concern that so many of the renowned players need to hear that message.

Jurgen Klopp named Florian Wirtz in his first squad as Germany manager and has said that fans must refrain from expecting “special moments” from the Liverpool playmaker as a matter of course.

Of Wirtz, he said: “I think he’s the player who covered the most ground at Liverpool this season, so the willingness is absolutely there.

“We have to move away from the idea that we need to see special moments from him. He is there to help us as a team. We have to make sure that Flo feels comfortable with us.”

Wirtz has delivered seven goals and 11 assists in his 54 Liverpool appearances.

Adam Smith, 35, played for Iraola 81 times and he admitted his former manager’s visit to the Vitality will be a sentimental affair. He said: “It’s going to be an emotional day for everyone I think, [for] our ex-manager and some of our players that have played under him, but we’ll be up for the game for sure.”

Bournemouth signed Truffert from Rennes in the summer of 2025 to replace Kerkez – who had just joined Liverpool – and the left-back has been a revelation at the Vitality. So much so that this week he earned himself a call-up to Zinedine Zidane’s first France squad.

Truffert topped the charts for most overlapping runs by any player in Europe’s top five leagues last season and laid on five assists.

Speaking before his return to the South Coast, Iraola said: “I know where we are going [the Vitality], and I know the stats they have there [unbeaten in 12 matches], not only in their stadium, overall, I think if you see the games they’ve lost in a long while, you realise how difficult it is to beat Bournemouth.

“But, I suppose I also have the advantage that I know them very well, they also have the advantage that they know me very well, so you never know who has more advantage in that sense.

He added: “On a personal side, I’m very much looking forward to meet them [his former players], to hug them. It’s players that I love, staff that I’ve been working with who I appreciate so much, and I was pushing for them [against Real Sociedad] when they were playing their first European game. I wish them all the best, but there is another part, which is the most important one right now that we need to go there and win.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool and Bournemouth as Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium for the first time since his big move up north. The Basque propelled Bournemouth to new heights, guiding the club into Europe and his successor, Marco Rose, ensured they made a winning start to life on the Continent by defeating Real Sociedad in midweek.

Previewing Iraola’s Vitality Stadium return, Craig Beazley, host and creator of the Up The Cherries In All Departments podcast, said: “We’ve now got the Andoni Iraola return … Andoni is very much a legend really, there should be a statue of Sir Eddie Howe and Sir Andoni Iraola [outside the ground] as well.”

Across three seasons, Iraola guided Bournemouth to 12th, ninth and sixth in the Premier League, winning 47 of his 127 matches in charge (37 per cent).

Liverpool are still acclimatising to his exacting style of play and their results suggest as much. They are 10th in the table having drawn three and won one, impressing in flashes but struggling to maintain consistently productive final-third patterns and pressing structures. Deploying Ronald Araújo at right-back has proved effective, though, with Liverpool conceding just two goals in their last four matches.

The Cherries are searching for their first Premier League win of the season and have retained the 4-2-3-1 shape from the Iraola days, with Rose preferring a similarly vertical attacking strategy. They continue to leverage their strengths in transitions and in wide areas as Adrien Truffert rains in crosses for any one of Bournemouth’s exuberant frontline to pounce on.

Elsewhere, Manchester City welcome Sunderland, who also secured a Europa League win during the week, to the Etihad while in-form Leeds United host Crystal Palace knowing a win would lift them into the top four.

#1456. Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

A study suggests that people are being misdiagnosed as having obesity with a metric known as the body mass index (BMI).Credit: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty

Clinicians have debated for years whether body mass index (BMI) — a metric derived from a person’s height and weight — is the best way to define and diagnose obesity. Now, an approach that measures waist circumference and focuses more closely on excess body fat has proved to be better than BMI at predicting a person’s risk of death.

New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health

New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health

An analysis of data collected from more than 800,000 individuals found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The study was published today in Nature1.

Physicians know that BMI — calculated by dividing a person’s weight by the square of their height — doesn’t accurately reflect body composition. For example, a muscular person might have an elevated BMI but have little body fat. The latest study “reinforces that BMI is not a good measure of obesity at the individual level and is not good in terms of predicting who is going to develop cardiometabolic disease in the long term”, says Cátia Martins, an obesity researcher at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

But given how simple it is to calculate BMI, it remains the most widely used tool to classify obesity.

A person is usually diagnosed with obesity if they have a BMI of 30 or higher. The approach presented in the study — called the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, or CAD-obesity — goes beyond BMI, combining it with measures, such as waist circumference, that are linked to excess body fat. Physicians know that when fat tissue is preferentially stored in the abdominal area, it is associated with more negative health consequences than when it’s stored elsewhere, Martins says.

Why BMI is flawed — and how to redefine obesity

Why BMI is flawed — and how to redefine obesity

Under the CAD-obesity system2, first proposed last year, people with obesity who also have at least one of 18 specific health problems — including heart failure and sleep apnoea — are classified as having ‘clinical obesity’. This indicates that excess fat is harming their organs and tissues. Those with obesity but none of these health problems are classified as having ‘preclinical obesity’, in which a person has excess fat but their organs are functioning normally.

“We did not know until now whether or not this new framework had implications in the real world and a prognostic value,” says Francesco Rubino, a weight-loss surgeon at King’s College London who led the effort to create the system and is a co-author of the Nature paper.

But Rubino and his colleagues proved the system’s worth by examining medical records from four large groups of people in China, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States. They used data from three of those cohorts, in which more than 50,000 deaths occurred over up to 15 years, to determine whether BMI or the CAD-obesity system was a better indicator of elevated mortality risk.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5

Read the related Clinical Briefing, ‘Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method’.

And listen to a related podcast that discusses this study here.

#1455. Phelan's Momentum Ahead of Spurs Test

Coming off the back of a 6-0 victory at Goodison last night, Scott Phelan's Blues head into this weekend’s clash against Spurs with a four-game unbeaten streak and unrivalled confidence.

On last night’s cup match against Durham, the head coach highlighted the squad’s “top of their game” performance. Everton dominated possession for the full 90 minutes of the game, using additional "time on the ball" to net six goals – with a hattrick from Japanese forward Yuka Momiki.

Phelan now hopes that the team can gain momentum from the impressive victory.

"Last night was an opportunity to show the top of our game and have a lot of the ball," said Phelan in his pre-match press conference on Thursday afternoon. "That will hopefully give the players a confidence boost."

On the WSL season so far, Phelan commended the players' “excellent” performance in a series of “challenging” fixtures. The last two weekends seeing the Blues hold a strong fort against high-flying Manchester United and Chelsea, bringing both matches to a draw.

"It has been a positive last three fixtures," he continued. "We knew this run of fixtures would be challenging, but to see the players performing has been excellent.

The 2026/27 season has also seen the introduction of the Subway Players Cup. An excited Phelan maintains that this is a “positive addition” to the league, as “more games and opportunities” are available to players.

"It enhances the league so there's more games and more opportunities. Overall. it has been a positive addition.

The overall strong form of the team has seen them progress further in the league, with the former Under-21s captain noting that this was one of the “challenges” they were up against this season.

"Four games, four wins," he stated. "That gives us a real strong chance of progressing which was one of the challenges for this season.

Saturday’s game sees Everton face Spurs away from home, with no fresh injuries in the squad heading into this weekend.

Recovering centre-back Megan Finnigan started in Wednesday’s cup match, with Phelan saying he is "pleased to see her getting 90 minutes on the pitch after a long time injured."

Last season saw Everton beat the Londoners 2-1 away from home. The Blues’ head coach is confident that his squad can bring fierce competition and good form into this weekend’s reunion.

#1454. Bruno Fernandes snubs second new contract offer from Man United in early headache for incoming manager Mauricio Pochettino - with star free to talk to foreign clubs as early as January

Published: 18:28 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 14:42 EST, 13 November 2026

Bruno Fernandes has rejected a new contract at Manchester United against the turbulent backdrop of the departure of head coach Michael Carrick.

The Manchester United captain publicly questioned the former manager's tactics after his side's Champions League thrashing at the hands of Como, and has struggled to find form this season.

Discussions are believed to have started between Fernandes and Man United over the summer, on the heels of a strong campaign which saw him named Men's PFA Player of the Year.

But after an initial proposal from the club is thought to have been rejected by the midfield talisman, Fernandes has now snubbed a second deal with improved terms, in what could be an early headache for incoming manager Mauricio Pochettino.

The Portuguese international's contract is set to expire in June 2027, which means that if the club and player fail to agree fresh terms, Fernandes will be free to discuss a summer move with clubs abroad as early as the January transfer window.

The club may yet seek to trigger the 12-month extension in Fernandes' contract, but will continue talks over aspects including his salary and the length of his new deal as they are keen for him to stay.

Bruno Fernandes has rejected a second set of terms from Manchester United as the club seeks to pin him down to a new deal

The club captain inked his latest terms in 2024 with his contract set to expire next June

Man United currently sit in the relegation zone after a 40-year worst-ever start to the season, and announcing a new deal for Fernandes might have given the club an important boost of morale during a difficult international break.

Fernandes was brought back into the fold after going through a brief period of being frozen out of Carrick's squad following his incendiary comments following defeat in Italy last month.

Fernandes, who is usually very deliberate in what he says in the media, was scathing in his criticism of coaches after the Como debacle.

'It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball,' he said.

'But sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work.'

His post-Como interview was widely condemned by fans and pundits alike, with Gary Neville lamenting: 'If that's your captain saying that, imagine what they're saying in the dressing room behind closed doors when no one's listening. That's horrific.'

He also told Fernandes to 'read the room' and accused him of being an 'excuse merchant' on his podcast.

Fernandes was left on the bench for Man United's next Premier League appointment, a loss to Bournemouth, before returning to the starting XI against Chelsea the following matchday.

After Man United's comeback win against Roma, Fernandes was defiant in his post-match remarks as he stressed that he had not been sanctioned for undermining Carrick with his initial interview.

'The club needed that win. The players needed that win. It is something we needed as a group of players and staff,' he said. 'We have been working so hard to get out of this situation together. It has been tough. There has been a lot of speculation in the media.

Fernandes was publicly critical of his former head coach Michael Carrick last month but was later adamant that he had not held clear-the-air talks with him

'A lot of lies around many things that have happened at this club, between me and the manager, like that we have cleared the air. Nothing like that happened.

'The manager took a decision of making myself on the bench because I wasn't performing. And that's fair.

'Everyone felt like that was a punishment for the words that I had [after Como]. And if it was, it was right.

'The manager makes the decisions. I have to accept it. I have to go forward with that. It doesn't change the belief I have in the manager, the staff and every player at this club.

'And it doesn't change my aim to win every f***ing game that I have ahead of me.'

Fernandes' sabre-rattling was ultimately unable to keep Carrick in his job however, with the former club captain finally sacked on Thursday after an agonising three-day wait.

Man United's hierarchy, notably chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, have come under fire from the fanbase and within the club for their treatment of the departing coach, with Carrick taking two days of training at Carrington as they mulled his sacking.

Wilcox and Berrada jetted to Monaco earlier this week to meet with Ineos chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe and discuss the departure of Carrick, with the club's Glazer ownership ratifying the decision to replace him with United States national team coach Pochettino.

Daily Mail Sport reported on Thursday evening that staff members inside the club have been upset with the protracted sacking, which has been deemed disrespectful of Carrick's status as a club legend.

#1452. Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Minimalist biotechnology companies that have just a handful of employees — or even as few as one — are becoming more feasible with the rise of artificial-intelligence tools.Credit: Getty

How many scientists does it take to discover a drug?

The question came to the fore after news that a biotechnology company armed with an artificial-intelligence assistant, two promising drug leads and just one full-time human employee had been acquired by San Francisco-based Anthropic as part of the AI giant’s expansion into biomedical science.

AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

In truth, it took many human scientists to develop the molecules that are the mini-company’s star products: two antibodies that are still in the early stages of development and were designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy. The company, Mithril Medicine in Cambridge, Massachusetts, also hired part-time consultants to advise on the project, and paid at least five contract research organizations to conduct experiments. Many more researchers will be needed to carry the drug further, especially if it eventually enters clinical trials. “It takes a village to develop a drug,” says Jeb Keiper, a partner at Third Rock Ventures, a venture-capital firm in Boston, Massachusetts.

But the news sparked a wave of discussions about whether the one-person biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future. “We will see more and more of these small teams that are enabled by AI,” says James Zou, a computer scientist who works on biomedical applications of AI at Stanford University in California. “They will be very powerful for identifying good opportunities and moving quickly.”

Itsy-bitsy biotechs are not a new concept. Entrepreneur Matt Davidson started his first biotech company in 2013, nearly a decade before ChatGPT’s public debut. Davidson kept the roster trim for years, with only two full-time employees until the drug he was developing was ready to enter late-stage clinical testing. The company never had a physical laboratory, Davidson says. All the lab work was contracted out.

His current company, Azora Therapeutics in Los Angeles, California, has a whopping five employees. He uses AI more for summarizing reports than for scientific discovery and says that AI tools have made tiny biotechs more efficient. “We use consultants a little bit less than we used to,” he says.

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Mithril Medicine leaned more heavily on AI than Azora does, and tasked Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude with helping to analyse data and suggesting next steps, as well as taming the piles of e-mails and paperwork that come from working with multiple contract research organizations. “What began as an exercise in staying lean evolved into the thesis for an entirely new operating model, which we now call Pipeline-in-a-Person,” wrote Cody Tranbarger, Mithril’s former chief executive and lone employee, on LinkedIn. (Tranbarger, who has worked for Anthropic since Mithril was absorbed into it, declined to speak to Nature, as did Anthropic.)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03640-9

Zhang, H. G., Eckmann, P., Miao, J., Mahon, A. B. & Zou, J. Science 394, eaeg6779 (2026).

#1451. Everton Duo Help England Reach Quarter-Finals

Jordan Pickford edged closer to a century of caps for the England national team on Thursday evening, with James Garner also featuring in a 2-1 victory over Croatia that booked passage to the UEFA Nations League quarter-final stage.

Confirmed by Thomas Tuchel as England’s continuing number one at the start of the international break, Pickford started at Wembley in his 94th senior Three Lions outing.

The spotlight for the evening, however, was firmly on Harry Kane. The Bayern Munich striker was fresh from picking up the Ballon D’Or and made yet more history by surpassing Peter Shilton’s long-held record of 125 England appearances.

Garner and Jarrad Branthwaite, meanwhile, were both on the bench, but only the former would take to the field.

By the time Tuchel made a triple substitution in the 77nd minute – with Garner replacing Arsenal captain Declan Rice in midfield – Kane had already restored England’s lead.

Morgan Rogers had given the hosts the advantage with a close-range finish in the first half, but an error from defender Jarrell Quansah allowed the Croatians to level on the hour mark.

Kane then converted from the spot five minutes later, before it looked to be a dream cameo from Garner as he found the back of the net himself, but a VAR check confirmed an offside in the build-up to deny a first senior international goal for Everton's 2025/26 Player of the Season.

Branthwaite remained an unused substitute in London and will be hoping for game time when England head to Madrid to take on World and European champions Spain in their final game in Group C.
