#1422. Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

It will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

At the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”

This was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

“It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9

Tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw

“Very difficult to understand. We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is the different to all the (other) tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”

Lewis Hamilton says this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

“The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”

“I love this energy [from the crowd]. Big, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”

A reminder that Isack Hadjar will drop from third to eighth after his grid penalty.

QUALIFYING CLASSIFICATIONCan't wait for Sunday! 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/qqi8hPDcKA

“It is fantastic. We have been trying many grand prix to get pole. Sometimes a bit closer than others but to finally get it, from where we started the season, pretty incredible. I am happy with today and, for sure, I am going to try and win tomorrow. When you start first, that is the target.”

Big disappointment that for Russell. After his win in Baku, where he said he finally felt hooked up to the car, he was desperate to build the momentum. P8, four places behind Antonelli, was not what he would have had in mind. Has it all to do in the race tomorrow.

Excellent (though not unexpected) pole for Verstappen, and a very good P2 for Hamilton. Could be some fireworks on the front row tomorrow.

*Hadjar’s three-place grid penalty will drop him down to eighth place for the race tomorrow.

Neither of the Red Bulls can improve in the first sector but it is those behind them who need significant improvements. The two Ferraris are going along nicely at the start of their final flying laps. Hadjar is unable to improve despite a purple final sector. Verstappen then goes fastest in the final sector and improves his advantage at the top.

Hamilton meanwhile went fastest in the middle sector and goes second fastest overall. Piastri cannot improve but stays ahead of Russell.

Norris is the final man across the line but is only fast enough for P6. That means that Verstappen takes pole in Malaysia, which is the first time this season that Red Bull have taken pole position. Hamilton is second with Hadjar third, although the Frenchman has a five-place grid penalty.

MAX VERSTAPPEN TAKES POLE FOR THE BAHRAIN GRAND PRIX IN MALAYSIA!! 👊#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/NgtaCAZacL

The two Red Bulls, who are one and two at the moment, will be the first two drivers across the line on these final efforts.

The other nine drivers in Q3 are in the pits so young Antonelli has the track to himself as he sets his one and only flying lap of Q3. He is over four tenths down on Verstappen through the first sector and has plenty of work to do.

The championship leader sets a decent middle sector where he loses no more time to Verstappen. As it stands he would put himself third before the others do their final runs. He comes across the line in P3 but will have the likes of Hamilton, Piastri, Leclerc, Norris and Russell trying to surpass him.

Russell is the first across the line and sets a time of a 1:36.032. He does not last long at the top as he is immediately displaced by Hadjar, who is half a second quicker.

Hamilton then comes over the line in second, just ahead of his teammate Leclerc. Piastri puts himself between the two Ferraris.

What about Verstappen? The man who won here the last time we were in Malaysia continues his great form today and goes quickest by more than three tenths.

Antonelli now heads out and will have the track to himself really. This is going to be the championship leader’s only flying lap of Q3.

Russell is the first man to head out for his first flying lap in Q3. Antonelli has remained in the pits with just one new set of softs remaining. Verstappen, who right now feels like the favourite for pole, will be one of the last across the line in these first attempts of Q3.

The fight for pole position in Sepang begins now as the green light is on at the end of the pit lane to get Q3 going.

Antonelli, due to that lap time deletion in Q2, has just one new set of softs for Q3, which could prove costly in his attempts to try and take pole.

P12 the best qualifying result of the season for Alonso. It was only his second time in Q2 after Hungary (P16).

I should add, P14 was also Lance Stroll’s best qualifying result of the season. His first outing in Q2 this year.

11. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls)12. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)13. Carlos Sainz (Williams)14. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)

With grid penalties already on their way, neither Colapinto nor Lindblad set lap times in Q2.

Verstappen, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris, Hadjar and Russell all remain in the pits. A bit of a risk for Russell down in eighth but his time should be enough to get into Q3.

Lindblad, who will start tomorrow’s race at the back of the grid after penalties, gives his teammate Lawson a tow down the back straight and it works as Lawson just sneaks into the top ten.

Can Bortoleto get back ahead though of Lawson? Yes he can and he will take the final place in Q3. Lawson thought he might be through but the tow was not enough.

Lindblad, who's taking a grid penalty for Sunday's race, gave team mate Lawson a tow but it wasn't quite enough to send the Kiwi into Q3#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/IMlrqg4ENv

As the young Italian starts his flying lap, there is no-one else out on track so no traffic. He is a lot more cautious at turn six this time than last time, when he had his lap time deleted.

He has not set blistering first and second sector times but a purple final sector puts him into second and the Italian is safely into Q3.

Plenty of other drivers are now heading around the track for their final flying laps of Q2.

11. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)12. Carlos Sainz (Williams)13. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)14. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)

Mercedes have put a brand new set of softs onto Antonelli’s car as he heads out promptly, with no lap time to his name so far. Antonelli is still disputing the lap deletion over team radio but his team tell him the images show he exceeded track limits. This is now a lot of pressure on the championship leader; any mistake now and he will not make Q3. His teammate Russell is only in seventh.

Antonelli was fourth fastest but has had his lap time deleted for exceeding track limits at turn six. That is a big moment in Q2 and could prove problematic if he gets into Q3. Antonelli appeared to be confused when he was told about his lap deletion over team radio but the on-board view looked pretty clear-cut.

Piastri then comes across the line in third.

Here's the moment Kimi ran wide 👀#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/E0VdWdBt8x

The Dutchman looks in a great spot at the moment to take pole position today and his 1:35.696 is very quick. He is nearly four tenths quicker than Antonelli.

How about the Ferraris? Leclerc was quickest in the middle sector but is nearly three tenths down on Verstappen. Hamilton puts himself into third place. Russell is more than half a second down on Verstappen.

Verstappen has been shown a black and white flag for driving unnecessarily slowly. I doubt he will get a grid penalty for that but it will be a warning for the Dutchman.

Anyway, the drivers, other than Colapinto and Alonso, are on flying laps, with Verstappen currently fastest inthe first sector.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and the second part of qualifying is under way. Like the start of Q1, it is hardly a stampede to go out.

17. Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)18. Oliver Bearman (Haas)19. Esteban Ocon (Haas)20. Alex Albon (Williams)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

The Aston Martin of Stroll improves significantly from 20th and is set to make Q2, as is his teammate Alonso. A bit of a surprise to see the Aston Martins improve and make it into Q2.

Go Fernando! 🤩 Go Lance! 🤩First double Q2 appearance this season 🙌#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/xjiWYv6ycr

That has seen the Audi of Hulkenberg drop into the drop zone and the German is out. For contrast, his teammate improves to go into eighth place! Hulkenberg had a big lock up into turn 14, which proved very costly.

As it stands, eight of the top nine are remaining in the garage. Russell is in ninth and has not gone out but Gasly above him in eighth has. You would imagine Russell is perfectly safe.

17. Esteban Ocon (Haas)18. Alex Albon (Williams)19. Oliver Bearman (Haas)20. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

Ocon, in 17th, is quite far off Hulkenberg in 16th and needs more than four tenths to usurp him.

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

The two Ferraris are on medium tyres but Leclerc still puts himself into second place. He is then displaced by Hamilton, who slots in behind Verstappen. Good times from the Ferraris on the mediums.

What about the McLarens? Norris goes sixth fastest but is more than six tenths down on Verstappen. Then comes Piastri, who goes fourth fastest, just under four tenths off Verstappen.

Arguably the three favourites for pole; Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen, are all on flying laps.

The first sector goes the way of Verstappen, who is purple, and then the Dutchman goes purple in the middle sector.

Antonelli is two tenths faster than his teammate Russell but Verstappen is over half a second quicker than the Mercedes. Hadjar is then second fastest to show the pace in the Red Bull this weekend.

Most of the teams waited and waited to come out and then suddenly lots of drivers are sent out, resulting in a queue in the pits! With the high track temperatures and high degradation, the drivers are crawling around on their out laps to preserve these soft tyres.

Bumper to bumper in the pit lane! #F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/ff8JO9kB1g

The two Haas drivers have a free track to themselves whilst everyone else bides their time. In theory, as the hour of qualifying goes on, the track temperature should decrease and the more rubber that is laid down the faster the track should get.

Finally, just before the two Haas drivers finish their first flying laps, the rest of the grid is starting to emerge, led by the Mercedes duo.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and Q1 is officially under way. The two Haas drivers are the first to head out. Other than that, it is a quiet start to Q1.

The top four teams; Mercedes, Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren, all have a genuine chance of taking pole in Sepang today. I think the true favourites though have to be the Mercedes duo and Max Verstappen but with how close it between all four of the teams you cannot rule anything out.

It is 33 degrees celsius air temperature, with the track temperature up at 58 degrees.

Not long to wait now until qualifying begins. It is hot, humid and dry in Sepang right now. As we know in Malaysia, the weather can change quickly and thunderstorms can roll in quite quickly but it looks like today’s qualifying will be a dry one. This will be one of if not the hottest qualifying sessions of the season, so much so that we are seeing umbrellas going up to get some shade from the sun rather than sheltering from any rain.

This will be important to consider after qualifying finishes as there will be some shuffling around:

Isack Hadjar (Red Bull): five-place grid penalty- new internal combustion engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): ten-place grid penalty- new engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): five-place grid penalty- causing a collision in BakuArvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls): back of the grid- complete power unit change

Hadjar has looked good since returning from his wrist injury so could be fighting it out near the front of the grid, although his five-place penalty will drop him down. We know Lindblad will be at the back and is very likely to be joined there by Colapinto, who is not going to be qualifying high up in the top ten in his Alpine.

Haas have announced that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

TGR Haas F1 Team and Esteban Ocon will part ways at the conclusion of the 2026 season. With plenty of racing ahead, our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year.#HaasF1 #F1 pic.twitter.com/4iQAuqnSyA

Aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Aston Martin Aramco confirms Lance and Fernando will continue as the team's drivers in 2027. Read more: ​https://t.co/ePyjJdyAIB pic.twitter.com/VogFUEbNxy

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to issue a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti said. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso)

With Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

This race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

#1421. My Story: O’Brien's Diabetes Diagnosis & Journey Into Football

To mark World Diabetes Day, we revisiting a chat with Everton defender Jake O’Brien, who sat down to discuss his experiences with the condition.

A Republic of Ireland international, O'Brien also covered a wide range of topics including his journey into professional football and an impressive sporting background.

O’Brien was diagnosed with type one diabetes aged 16 – and recalling that time, he explained: “There were a few weeks when I was ill. I was losing a lot of weight and was very tired. I was drinking eight or nine litres of water a day.

“I realised something wasn’t right. I went to the doctor’s and they sent me up to hospital and diagnosed me with it. My pancreas, basically, doesn’t work; it doesn’t produce insulin.

"It’s a genetic thing, I suppose, but in that sense, no one in my family has ever had it."

#1420. Why Bukayo Saka's England spot is suddenly under threat: Clocking up the miles has made Arsenal star a fitness concern - while his rival Morgan Rogers is hitting top gear: CRAIG HOPE

Published: 08:57 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 09:21 EST, 14 November 2026

Five seasons ago, Bukayo Saka clocked up 3,000 Premier League minutes for Arsenal. Morgan Rogers appeared in just 217 for Bournemouth, then of the Championship. The pair are the same school age. Yet, back then, one was a young man at the very top of the game, the other was a boy wondering where, and how, he would ever get a game.

In the same week that Rogers, a Manchester City junior, made his only league start during an unhappy loan season on the south coast - in a goalless draw at Peterborough - Saka was scoring in a 3-1 win in the North London derby. They were on very different flight paths.

Today, the ascent of Rogers compares with, dare we say it, the gradual descent of Saka. His supporters will contest that trajectory. They can point to his two goals for England in Croatia last month, his hat-trick in the 6-4 World Cup bronze-medal victory over France and, of course, his Premier League winner’s medal. Their argument has merit, as does any that defends a player of such talent.

Except, this is not about ability. It is about durability. It is about mileage and the fear that, at 25 years old, a near 400 career games are weighing heavy. Rogers, quite remarkably, has played 10,000 fewer Premier League minutes. He is, to borrow horse-racing parlance, unexposed and open to improvement.

Until three years ago, this was Saka. He started 87 consecutive Premier League games for Arsenal, a club record, and was getting better season on season - seven, 12, 15 and 20 were his goals tallies from 2021 to 2024. He was both the present and future of the England team.

Bukayo Saka's starting spot in the England XI is now under serious threat ahead of Euro 2028

England are flourishing with Chelsea's Morgan Rogers (right) occupying the right-hand side

And yet now, increasingly among those who obverse and are close to the England camp - including, you suspect, Thomas Tuchel - there is a feeling of Saka’s presumed starting jersey being under serious threat. In fact, you wonder if the threat has already passed. Does the position on the right of England’s forward line, with a view to Euro 2028, now belong to Rogers?

This, it should be said, is as much about the exceptional development of Rogers, who will again start on the right here in Spain on Sunday night. But there is another, more uncomfortable possibility, and that is of Saka’s very best days belonging to those North London derbies of yesterday, not tomorrow. He is currently injured with a thigh strain and faces several more weeks on the sidelines.

I was in the room with Tuchel at the World Cup pre-camp in Florida when he revealed, to some surprise, ’Bukayo is just not there yet. Some things are missing’. We had assumed Saka was fit after arranging private sessions in the wake of the Champions League final. The head coach, however, said it would be ‘very unlikely’ that Saka, nursing Achilles discomfort, would be able to start and finish all of England’s matches, and so it proved. He did not start and finish any before the France kick-about, a match that should have been played at Miami Beach, not Miami Stadium.

In the days prior to the semi-final against Argentina, Saka told Tuchel and medical staff he was ready to start. Tuchel went with Rogers on the right and Saka was an unused substitute. After his treble three days later, Saka spoke of his frustration with his playing time in North America.

Throughout the tournament, Tuchel rejected the idea of the Arsenal man being ‘the saviour’, as it was put to him by one colleague following the group-stage goalless draw with Ghana.

‘I’m not engaging in that,’ he told us. ‘It’s not like Bukayo comes back and everything is solved.’

And Tuchel was right. Saka did a lot of good - three assists in the tournament proper - but it felt like he was existing in moments, much like at Euro 2024. Gone was that whiplash speed taking him through defensive lines, the drag and dribble that defenders knew was coming but could do little about. Club-mate Noni Madueke had that explosion, just not Saka’s end product. Combine the two and we had a player. It was why, come the semis, Tuchel went with Rogers.

Recurring injuries and setbacks have plagued the Arsenal winger over the past few seasons

He was once viewed as England's present and future - but has suffered from a gradual decline

To revisit our Daily Mail Sport tournament ratings, in which Saka scored 6/10, we recorded: ‘Fitness issues should offer some context, but this was a version of Saka unrecognisable from the player we thought was up there with Kane and Bellingham when it came to being a game-changer. He did provide three assists, including a lovely cross for the opener in Mexico, but never appeared to fully trust his body. Has a bit to prove when back to full fitness.’

Will he ever, though, regain a consistent level of fitness, strength and sharpness that allows him to impact - again, consistently - like he once did? Just last week, Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta admitted the club were struggling to identify the underlying reason for injuries which total double figures in three years.

‘We have openly discussed a lot of things with him to understand what could possibly have gone wrong,’ said Arteta. ‘But the reality probably is that unfortunately we don’t know.’

Saka, to return to horse racing, has the form in the book, but that is the concern. There is, perhaps, too much form at too young an age, especially when coupled with a game reliant on acceleration and intensity.

Rogers himself still has a lot to prove, not least because of his £117million transfer from Aston Villa to Chelsea in the summer. With that, though, he has grown. That much was evident by him taking centre stage against Croatia on Thursday night despite the presence of Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham. Previously, you suspected Rogers was waiting for the leading men to hand him his script.

His tendency to come infield will suit Tuchel, too. Kane the quarterback, as we saw at Wembley, leaves a space to populate and exploit. Rogers had more touches in the penalty area than any other player, including the one for his opening goal. And if Anthony Gordon, on the opposite flank, is the one with chalk on his boots, Rogers muddying his in the goalmouth is what the team needs.

Meanwhile, Rogers has hit top gear at Chelsea and become a key man under Thomas Tuchel

This debate, Saka versus Rogers, is not one that should keep Tuchel awake at night. It is a nice problem to have - the hope that Saka will return to his best, the expectation that Rogers is still to realise his.

On Sunday, at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid, Rogers has another opportunity to further his claims. He has come a long way since a drab Wednesday night at Peterborough’s London Road in 2021. It is, though, the distance yet travelled that is most exciting.

#1419. How to avoid aliens and live

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mark Arnold writes speculative fiction with a broken remote in one hand and a sociology paper in the other.

Issued by the Unified Earth Government, Office of Cosmic Silence

Following the Cascade Incident, the Yarrow Misunderstanding and what is now formally called The Cake Problem, these protocols have been aggressively revised. Read carefully. Your late predecessors did not.

Nothing. All unknown alien lifeforms are extremely dangerous, and death is the usual First Contact result — for the human. Most personnel therefore prefer attending the Second Contact proceedings.

Suddenly remember you have an important appointment on the other side of the Galaxy. Do not answer. You are a rock. If you must answer, say “I am a rock.”

Ask them to state the nature of their emergency. If no emergency, put them on HOLD.

“It’s complicated.” “Around.” Never name a location you would like to keep. You are from nowhere. Continue this trend. Geography is a vulnerability. Wave in a vague direction and mumble, “Over thereabouts …”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Friendliness is a hunting strategy. Your cat is friendly. The alien’s dead bird on the doorstep will be you.

Do not listen to your Engineers. They will say it would be cool. It isn’t.

The first alien species we ever contacted bred by laying eggs in your chest. Bring protection. Flamethrowers are kept in Storage B12.

Nothing good responds instantly. Delay your reply. Aim for disinterest, not malfunction. You are busy doing nothing elsewhere. Maintain that illusion.

You will. That’s how we lost Star Base 2.

No. You are, if a member of the Core, body count. Be a version that could belong anywhere and nowhere at the same time.

They will not define ‘this’. Do not ask. Undefined ‘this’ cannot be repeated and cannot be tracked. Leave it unresolved. Agree but do not fix a specific date. Do not, under any excuse, use the word ‘date’.

Decline. Do not swallow alien embryos. They taste of regret.

Quarantine. Two weeks minimum. Do not assume the thing wearing their face remembers your birthday.

No. Ask about their breathing requirements. Then say, “Oh, sorry, we don’t breathe that,” and change the subject immediately. Do not revisit the topic.

They are always the last of their kind. The last of its kind has a lot of free time and a lot of anger. Do not become its hobby.

You will. Internalize it. You have practice. Panic is normal. Displaying it is optional and discouraged. Don’t be a target.

You are still breathing and they do not know where the rest of us are. That is considered a success under current guidelines. Survival is the only metric.

#1418. The four problems Mauricio Pochettino needs to fix at Man United: From big names causing unrest in the dressing room to an issue which plagued Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick before him, these are the items top of his Old Trafford in-tray

Published: 21:00 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 10:51 EST, 14 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino will see out his final two games as US national team boss with a double-header against Haiti before starting work at Manchester United on Wednesday.

The 54-year-old won’t have any time to waste with a daunting first game against United’s bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday followed by a European clash with Sporting Lisbon in Portugal three days later.

With United languishing in the Premier League relegation zone and 17th in the Champions League standings, it’s clear why Pochettino has been brought in to replace Michael Carrick on a two-and-a-half-year contract.

Daily Mail Sport looks at the most pressing matters in Pochettino’s in-tray at Carrington as the former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss and his backroom staff head for Manchester...

Mauricio Pochettino is the new manager of Manchester United - but the problems he has to fix are already piling up

It sounds obvious, but winning games to get United out of the Premier League drop zone has to be the first priority.

Everything at a football club flows from the results on the pitch, and United’s humiliating decline this season has had ramifications throughout Old Trafford and Carrington.

The players are clearly low on confidence which has only exacerbated the team’s dismal performances and brought just one win in 10 Premier League games, against newly-promoted Ipswich – United’s worst start in 40 years.

Diogo Dalot is a prime example, after fans cheered his substitution in the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa last weekend, and the defender cut a crestfallen figure as he left Old Trafford to go on international duty with Portugal.

The Stretford End also turned on the players as the atmosphere turned toxic after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth at the end of last month, having vented their anger towards the club’s ownership – the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – as well as chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox at every opportunity.

That won’t go away anytime soon, but a winning team will at least take some of the sting out of the situation if appointing Pochettino can give United a ‘bounce’ and divert attention back onto the pitch.

United players are low on confidence, not least Diogo Dalot (left) whose substitution was cheered by his own fans against Aston Villa

The United team were also lambasted by the Stretford End after the 3-0 loss to Bournemouth last month

Carrick enjoyed a good start, losing just two of his 17 games in charge in the second half of last season to earn a two-year contract, but United struggled under him this term due to a combination of poor recruitment, injuries and lack of fitness.

These are all issues that Pochettino must try to put right. There is little he can do about recruitment until the January transfer window opens and United have a chance to atone for their mistake in not signing cover at left back and centre forward last summer, which backfired spectacularly when both Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko picked up injuries.

He can, however, try to get more out of United’s £155million midfield signings Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again – Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, and a United squad that was good enough to finish third in the Premier League last season.

Injuries have been a major problem with the hamstring strain that will keep Baleba out of action for Pochettino’s first few weeks in charge just the latest setback.

As well as Shaw, Sesko, Baleba and long-term casualty Manuel Ugarte, United have also lost Amad Diallo, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Lisandro Martinez, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui for parts of this season.

Pochettino must get more out of United’s £155million midfield signing Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again

United have struggled to keep up with their opponents since the opening day - a lack of fitness has plagued every manager since Ole Gunnar Solskjaer

The good news for Pochettino is that Shaw and Rashford are hoping to be fit for Anfield, while Matthijs de Ligt is available again after a year out with back problems. However, Sesko’s absence until the new year leaves the new boss without his most natural source of goals.

Fitness is another matter and United have looked short of it since the opening-day defeat at Hull City amid concerns that the coaching levels dropped off under Carrick and were too relaxed.

They covered 120.8 kilometres against Villa – the most in a league game under Carrick – and Pochettino will demand that and a whole lot more as he increases the work-rate among his new squad.

It’s a problem that has hindered a succession of United bosses going back to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and the Argentine must find a way to drill a better work ethic into United.

The problems at United this season have inevitably led to unrest in the dressing room, with the biggest issue centred around captain Bruno Fernandes.

News that Fernandes has rejected United’s latest contract offer has come as no surprise given his dramatic change in fortunes from last season, and Pochettino must find a way to get arguably United’s best player back in form and onside.

Having set a new Premier League record for assists and picked up a string of player of the year awards last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off a cliff as he struggled with an injury sustained at the World Cup, and he suffered the rare indignity of being benched for the loss to Bournemouth.

Never one to hide his mood very well, the 32-year-old criticised Carrick’s tactics after the Champions League defeat by Como in what was a major blow to his head coach.

Never one to hide his mood very well, Bruno Fernandes has been disgruntled of late and rejected United's offer of a new contract

Lisandro Martinez looks to be headed for the exit door - although the arrival of his fellow Argentine Pochettino may help things

While the United hierarchy will try to persuade Fernandes to sign a new deal in keeping with their reduced wage structure and the fact he will turn 33 next year, Pochettino has to find a way of relighting the fire in his skipper.

Whether the club will make as much effort to keep Lisandro Martinez as he comes towards the end of his contract remains to be seen after another member of United’s leadership team took aim at Wilcox’s recruitment after the defeat by Atletico Madrid. It is said to have caused an angry clash between Martinez and summer signing Tielemans on the way back from Spain.

Martinez looks to be heading for the Old Trafford exit, but it will be interesting to see if the arrival of his compatriot Pochettino – a combative Argentine centre back in much the same mould as a player – has an impact on that.

As a former defender, Pochettino won’t need telling that leaking 15 goals in the last five games simply isn’t good enough. United have now let in 30 in all competitions this season, the most of any club in Europe’s top five leagues apart from Lens.

They have been appalling at the back, conceding in the opening seconds to Atletico, Como and Villa. Had they been able to hold out and prevent late equalisers against Everton and Tottenham, the additional four points would have them 12th in the table rather than in the relegation zone.

A revolving door of makeshift left backs in the absence of Shaw and Dorgu, De Ligt’s belated comeback and Martinez’s needless red card at Chelsea haven’t helped.

Goalkeeper Senne Lammens, so composed last season, looks considerably more shaky behind a leaky and ever-changing back-four, and had arguably his worst game against Villa last weekend.

Pochettino couldn’t ask for a tougher first test than going to Anfield, and knows that United will have to start by being solid at the back.

#1417. Mauricio Pochettino's Man United SQUAD AUDIT: Axe EIGHT stars, new role for the attacker he's 'always liked' and who could be his new Dele Alli... now give YOUR player-by-player verdict

Published: 07:00 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 11:11 EST, 14 November 2026

Walking into a club in turmoil is nothing new for Mauricio Pochettino.

He arrived at Southampton with the Saints three points clear of the relegation zone. Tottenham Hotspur were crying out for some leadership after Andre Villas-Boas and Tim Sherwood's spells, while Chelsea picked up Pochettino in 2023 on the back of their lowest league finish for more than 25 years.

Now it's Manchester United that require what Victor Wanyama once described as Pochettino's 'magic touch' – and they need it quick as they sit in the relegation zone with ten games played. Pochettino remains weeks removed from the January transfer window and has a number of first-team regulars out with long-term injuries, so his reputation of improving the players at his disposal will be put to the test.

He has developed a reputation for placing faith in youth – while at Tottenham, Pochettino handed 12 debuts to players aged 21 or under, more than any other manager.

Money will be tight and United look almost certain to miss out on next season's Champions League, which will make squad development significantly harder, so Pochettino will have to make do and mend with a lot of the current underperforming crop of players.

With all that in mind, Daily Mail Sport runs the rule over the 36 players Pochettino will be inheriting when he walks through the door at Carrington next week.

And you can scroll to the end of the article to have your say on who should stay, and who should go...

Mauricio Pochettino will rapidly have to assess which Man United players to discard

Lammens won't be going anywhere. He is United's No 1 and despite a downturn in form this season, he's not become a bad goalkeeper overnight. Pochettino's trusted goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez will almost certainly replace Craig Mawson to bring some fresh ideas.

Jimenez focuses a lot on developing goalkeepers to be comfortable as sweepers and playing higher up. That is a sore spot in Lammens' game – recently exposed by Bournemouth striker Evanilson – but proper coaching should help develop Lammens, just like Jimenez developed Hugo Lloris.

A summer arrival from Leeds United as a back-up goalkeeper. Pochettino has more important issues than messing around with his No2.

Heaton is hugely popular at the club and while he doesn't play, he is viewed as a vital cog in the dressing room given his wealth of experience. He turns 41 later this season and has been busy preparing for life away from the pitch.

Heaton has completed courses on becoming a sporting director, as well as an executive leadership short course from Oxford University.

He also holds his goalkeeper coach B-Licence, A-Licence outfield, and a certificate of football management from UEFA.

Pochettino would be wise to keep Heaton in-house, even if not as a player. He is a respected figure who knows United inside out and that shouldn't be overlooked as Pochettino tries to build out a culture.

Senne Lammens (right) has made a shaky start to the season but will be going nowhere

Dalot is highly respected by every manager that works with him for the effort he puts in, something that can't always be said of some of his team-mates.

But he is woefully short of the required quality to take United forward and he is not a comfortable fit for Pochettino's ideals, either.

Pochettino gets width in his sides via the full backs and that requires a relentless runner – which Dalot is – having quality both defensively and in attack, which Dalot does not.

Malo Gusto, who is keen to leave Chelsea and could become a key target for United, spoke of how Pochettino developed his game in 2024 when he said: 'He helps us a lot. He has tried to show us the desire to win, to keep fighting against every team.

'He talks to us a lot about tactics, technique and everything. He is a good person as well. He tries to help us a lot on the pitch and off it. He is a good coach for this young team.

'He is here for this. He knows he has to wake up our mentality, to wake up our desire to win everything.'

United have neglected their back-line for years and it's time for a dramatic refresh, starting with shifting Dalot, who is under contract until 2028.

It is time for Man United to move on from Diogo Dalot - he is short of the quality required

Dalot has at least shown he has the engine to get up and down, which could offer a lifeline under Pochettino, but Mazraoui hasn't.

Full backs are essential to Pochettino's high-intensity, high press 4-2-3-1, and that's not a formula that suits Mazraoui's abilities.

Privately, sources close to the dressing room have suggested in recent weeks that Mazraoui, another under contract until 2028, is keen for a new challenge.

Overhauling the defence is one of the main topics of conversation among agents and players right now but De Ligt's future is secure at Old Trafford.

He is under contract until 2029, with the option of a further year, and many figures behind the scenes believe he can bounce back from such a long period out with injury to be a success.

De Ligt's injury record, as well as the fact he isn't a natural fit for Pochettino's idea of the perfect, mobile centre back, makes him an intriguing prospect.

Strong in physical duels, he could become a key squad player.

Maguire has taken more criticism than most during his time at United and deserves credit for how he has overcome it.

His contract expires in the summer, with the option of a further year, and Maguire has described playing for United as the 'ultimate honour' so is unlikely to agitate to leave.

That being said, Pochettino puts a lot of emphasis on recovery pace given the high line he has favoured in the past and the Argentine's tactics have routinely exposed centre backs in transition, with speed essential to masking shortcomings.

Maguire would undoubtedly struggle in that department and while his physical profile would appeal, he said earlier this year that he does not want to be kept around for 'sentimental value'.

'I love this club. But it's got to be right for myself, it's got to be right for the club as well,' Maguire said in March before a one-year extension was triggered.

'I don't want to be staying on sentimental value. I want to be staying because I want to be there and the club want me to drive the club forward still, and they feel like I've got a big part to play in it.'

The prospect of a diminishing role, with United planning multiple defensive reinforcements, may see both sides agree it's time for a change.

After seven years it may be time for Harry Maguire to move on, with his contract expiring

A player that looks to have one foot out the door after calling out director of football Jason Wilcox following the defeat by Atletico Madrid.

It's funny, almost, given Pochettino's arrival should suit Martinez down to the ground. In theory, he is the exact type of player his compatriot would implore his bosses to recruit.

Pochettino puts huge emphasis on passing out from the back and Martinez is the best in that category among United's centre backs.

Pochettino is also incredibly intense, something Martinez has been for some time at United, sometimes to the group's benefit and sometimes to its detriment.

The Argentine's contract expires in the summer and while there is an option to trigger a further year to avoid a World Cup winner walking away for nothing, the expectation is that he won't agree to a new one and his time at United is more likely than not drawing to a close.

He holds a desire to play in Spain and that may not vanish overnight. But if anyone can connect with Martinez about a longer-term role, it's a fellow Argentine.

Has the potential to be the biggest winner of the Pochettino appointment.

Pochettino's full-back-turned-winger style totally plays into Dorgu's hands given both his engine and his comfort playing higher up the pitch. Look at the development of Danny Rose – who played more games for Pochettino than any other player – and Kyle Walker, as well as Sergino Dest with the USA.

Dorgu has a lot of the attributes Pochettino craves while he also remains raw enough that intense, but targeted, coaching could improve him.

He should immediately become one of Pochettino's go-to men.

Where there are concerns around Maguire's ability to play in a system which squeezes everyone that bit higher up the pitch, Yoro should thrive.

He showed against Villa, with a chase down to deny Nicolas Jackson a run on goal, that he possesses the necessary recovery pace.

Pochettino's centre backs need to be strong passers and Yoro can improve in this area, although he has shown a willingness to dictate with long diagonals, as well as burst through lines as a ball-carrier.

United need five reliable centre backs in the squad moving forward and Yoro can establish himself as the No1.

Given Pochettino's track record with young players, he should be really excited at becoming a key piece of the puzzle under him.

A reunion… but one that may not last very long.

In a 2017 book about Pochettino, Shaw revealed his desire to work under him again and that wish has now come true.

'With Southampton he achieved the impossible,' said Shaw. 'We were one of the best footballing teams in the league... I do hope that I can play for him again one day. And I think he really wants me to play under him again.'

Pochettino used to call Shaw his 'son' and their relationship has stayed strong over the years.

But Pochettino is also a winner and will be acutely aware that Shaw cannot maintain the levels that Pochettino will require from his full backs after years of injury problems.

Sources close to the player have suggested the potential for a one-year extension given the relationship with Pochettino, even if those same sources believe the time is right for a fresh start.

A long servant but not one that can take United forward from this lowest of ebbs.

Luke Shaw and Pochettino enjoyed success together at Southampton but the reunion won't last long

Arriving as an Ineos project, United aren't going to cut their losses on Heaven just yet.

His strong passing ability will appeal to Pochettino and his coaches and he's worth a season of proper coaching to see how high or low his ceiling is.

Heaven can be reckless, particularly in his approach to tackling, but he's got a good physical profile and those who have worked with him have praised his approach to training and willingness to listen to coaches.

United are likely to go out and sign two new centre backs in the summer – at least they hope to – but Heaven should get a shot at development as a bit-part player.

Wholly ignored despite a left back crisis this season, Amass is widely expected to be out the door in January.

It is hard to blame him, either, given United's decision to keep him around has stunted his development.

Amass is a strong crosser of the ball and, in time, could develop into a full back in Pochettino's vision.

But neither Amass nor Pochettino will have time to wait and see. With a left back high on the shopping list, to go with Dorgu's expected ascension, this relationship shouldn't last too long.

Kamason has played both at right back and right wing for United's Under 21s and that plays massively into his hands in a bid to try and catch the eye of his new manager.

The United youngster is a well-rounded full back that constantly looks to get forward, all while not neglecting his defensive responsibilities.

Kamason has trained regularly with the first team in recent months and that could be a sign of things to come under Pochettino, too.

United rolled the dice on Leon a year ago in a deal worth an initial £3.3million – but the move has not worked out at all.

The 19-year-old hasn't come close to making a first-team appearance and his agent has even suggested they are getting itchy feet despite sub-par performances for United's Under 21s.

'If there isn't a plan to break into the first team between December and January, we'll look for a way out for him,' Leon's representative Renato Bittar admitted. 'A loan somewhere where he can compete, get playing time, and return to Manchester.'

Having observed the academy teams closer than most in recent seasons, Leon hasn't shown anywhere near enough to merit becoming a project player for Pochettino.

Mount left for United in the same summer Pochettino was hired by Chelsea, so their crossover was minimal.

How much say Pochettino had in that decision remains unclear, perhaps it was insignificant, but now they will finally work together.

Mount feels disposable, not least because he hasn't registered a single assist in the Premier League for United since joining in 2023 for £60million.

With so many options ahead of him in those inverted winger roles, and with Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans preferred as No 10s, Mount needs shifting.

Contract talks have stalled in recent weeks and months but an ambitious new manager could swing momentum back towards reigning Player of the Year Fernandes staying at Old Trafford.

The way Pochettino platformed Christian Eriksen and Dele Alli at Tottenham, as well as Cole Palmer at Chelsea, suggests Fernandes will get the role he needs to be at his very best.

Fernandes' mobility, and ability to run beyond his centre forward, is a strength, as is his vision to supply team-mates in open play and at set-pieces. If Fernandes plays well, so do United, generally. Pochettino favours inverted attackers, so Fernandes could even start off the left if his manager wanted to position Matheus Cunha or Tielemans more centrally.

'He's given me the freedom to play my stuff and I like it when he frees you because I feel I can express my stuff more,' Palmer said of Pochettino's coaching back in 2024.

'I'm loving it. Every day he's talking to you about different things, not just football things but life things as well. He's good at making you feel good and trying to get the best out of you.'

Pochettino's free-flowing approach could be exactly what is needed to keep Bruno Fernandes

Pochettino knows all about Santos having worked with him at Chelsea when he was a teenager still finding his way.

The reports at that time, during a pre-season tour in North Carolina and Philadelphia, were that Santos' profile appealed to Pochettino, only for the club to go ahead and sanction loan moves to Nottingham Forest and then Strasbourg.

Santos is a summer arrival for £50m and will get more time to find his role in this United side.

He has enough talent to become a reliable deputy to Baleba as the deep-lying midfielder when everyone is fully fit.

Tielemans is a high-IQ player that signed a five-year contract in the summer so, truthfully, won't be going anywhere.

That being said, Tielemans' running power isn't there and the demands of a Pochettino system, if he is still the same coach that bowed out at Chelsea, may make that secondary midfield role difficult.

It feels like Tielemans could be a specialist player that Pochettino uses in games where his side expect to dominate possession.

Tielemans' composure on the ball is superior to that of many of his team-mates and that's not a trait Pochettino will overlook quickly, even if he reportedly had reservations on a younger Tielemans when he was managing at Tottenham.

A big winner. The £70m summer signing needs to be used in the correct way to realise his potential and Pochettino's track record should be music to Baleba's ears.

Pochettino has typically liked one of his central midfielders to drop deep in possession to create a back three – see Eric Dier at Tottenham – and Baleba should be comfortable fulfilling that role.

Moises Caicedo and Wanyama are two other success stories in the deeper No6 role that Baleba should now thrive in under Pochettino's watch, with his combativeness and tackling making him a natural fit.

'Tactically, he has taught me a lot,' Wanyama previously said of Pochettino.

'Before, I was just thinking, "I'll just sit here and defend". But if you're playing for him, it's not only defending. You have to attack also. You have to know the right time. I have learned so much from him.'

Now it's time for Baleba to study up and take his game to the next level.

Carlos Baleba has a had a slow start to life at United but a managerial change could unlock his potential

It transpired that Pochettino wanted to make Ugarte his first signing at Chelsea, only for United to get in ahead of them for the Uruguayan.

Ugarte was all set to leave United in the summer were it not for a serious injury at the World Cup that left him sidelined for months.

Pochettino liked the profile of player he saw when Ugarte was scouted at Sporting Lisbon but he looks a different, far less effective, player in England.

Minds appear to be made up upstairs when it comes to moving on from Ugarte.

Where Baleba will need to drop deep, the other midfielder in Pochettino's system is the one who is expected to drive and bypass midfield blocks.

Pochettino will be acutely aware that Mainoo is extremely popular among United fans and while athleticism is often levelled against him as a weak point in his game, Pochettino will need to find a way of improving that while also nurturing his many talents.

Tottenham's Mousa Dembele was moulded by Pochettino from an attacking midfielder into a deep-lying controller, urged to dribble to break lines and open up the game.

Mainoo has many similar traits to others Pochettino has worked with, such as Weston McKennie with the US national team.

'They will get pushed in training more than the games they will be playing. It is all a mental thing,' former Southampton striker Rickie Lambert once said.

If Mainoo can come through the initial boot camp, he can flourish.

Kobbie Mainoo is one of United's top talents and will stay but has to improve his physicality

A better player than people give him credit for but one that really needs to put a full season together at first-team level to see where he is at.

That won't be under Pochettino at United but United, if they really believe he can be part of their future, need to find Fletcher a loan move where he can feature in 35-40 games.

Clubs in League One would be all over him.

The deep-lying midfielder that can drop in to form a back three is fundamental to how Pochettino wants to play and that's a style that would suit Tyler Fletcher, rather than the more attacking Jack.

Again, figures at United and up in Scotland, just want to see Fletcher get a run of games under his belt.

Kilmarnock wanted him in the summer, but United wanted to keep Fletcher in house.

If Pochettino and United really care about his career, he should be one of the first out the door on loan in January.

Senior academy figures are the most excited about Thwaites' potential, even if it would be unfair to expect him to make a big impact on the first team in the near future.

Technically his level is particularly high, a European pass-first, press-resistant game that will appeal to Pochettino and his coaches.

But physically there is a way to go, which should mean Thwaites is kept around as a project player.

Brought in as an Ineos project piece, after two mediocre loan spells in Switzerland with Lausanne, it's time to have Kone come back into the building and put him to work with a relentless coach like Pochettino.

Kone's twitchy game-style and desire to break through lines makes him something of a hybrid of players Pochettino has coached in the past.

Having watched him up close in the academy set-up before he went out on loan, and spoken to those who coached Kone then, it would be a big gamble for Pochettino to put his trust in him.

But Kone's ceiling feels sky high. It's time to see if he can go into the lab and come out as a Dembele-Wanyama hybrid.

Physically he has an advanced profile for his age but United have long preached that they want to take things slow as Orozco settles into life in England and gets a grip of the language.

He is neat and tidy on the ball and has shown an ability to zip passes through the lines but not enough to suggest an elevation to the first-team group.

Academy football doesn't develop players quickly enough so a carefully selected loan move, perhaps in a technical league like the Netherlands or Belgium, would be ideal.

He needs to look at how Pochettino used players like Lucas Moura and Eriksen in the past to see how he can take his game to the next level.

Cunha has a swagger about him that United like and while he was better suited to Ruben Amorim's system than he was Michael Carrick's, Pochettino's preference for narrow wide players, funnelling them into central areas while full backs create the width, means this managerial shift should play into his hands.

'Cunha is a maverick who does things that are hard to find in some players,' Amorim once said of the Brazilian.

'He plays with the ball, but he has an aura that can do something to the opponent's heads. And that is really important.'

It was recently suggested to Daily Mail Sport that a move for Rashford could be explored as early as January, with a desire to go back abroad.

A managerial change always puts things into flux and not least given that Pochettino said in 2022 that he'd 'always liked' Rashford, before adding: 'I think he's a great player. He just needs the confidence and for himself to believe, to put him at the top level. The quality is there for him.'

Pochettino is unlikely to have changed an opinion as solid as that one in the years that followed and so it will be curious to see if Rashford could become the athletic, pressing No9 in Benjamin Sesko's absence.

Rashford wants to feel the love and has shown what he can do when his confidence is high. It isn't right now but don't bet against Pochettino showing him that love.

Rashford has been linked with another move away but could become a pressing No 9

One of the more interesting profiles for Pochettino to consider.

On the face of it, Zirkzee lacks the intensity in the press and the mobility that Pochettino demands of his forwards.

Yet, Zirkzee can drop in, allowing the No10 to run in behind, which Pochettino values in a striker.

In the long term, expect Zirkzee to depart. In the short term, Pochettino may see him as a very specific tool to exploit certain opponents.

Tenacious defensively after improving immeasurably out of possession under Amorim, that's a big plus for Amad in the eyes of Pochettino.

He's among the glut of hybrid 10-wingers that United seem to stockpile and, once Sesko returns, Amad will find himself locked in a battle with Shea Lacey and Bryan Mbeumo for regular starts.

Amad's energy should give him the edge from day one to be a natural fit for Pochettino's high press.

Pochettino loves working with young players and Lacey is ready-made for that inverted winger style that the Argentine prefers, so he should be licking his lips at the prospect of more opportunities.

Lacey has played both off the right and as a No10 in academy teams and that stands him in good stead to operate in central areas, as well as isolate his full back one v one, which too many in this squad are not confident to do.

Lacey should be studying the development of Dele Alli under Pochettino and hoping he can bring his game on similarly.

Shea Lacey is (right) is a hugely promising youngster who will love working with Pochettino

Like Cunha, Mbeumo looked a more natural fit in Amorim's two-10s system and there are similarities that could put him back in those positions under Pochettino.

He's played a lot as a No 9 and may need to deputise there for the time being but the long-term dilemma for Pochettino will be the battle between Mbeumo, Amad and Lacey cutting in from the right.

It's one of the few areas of the pitch where there will be decent competition for places.

Mbeumo will need to find a position and master it or he may be caught in between roles.

Injured until, most likely, the end of January and so it will take some time for Pochettino to get his teeth into Sesko's development.

The Slovenian feels very close to Pochettino's ideal No9 profile given his athleticism, physicality in the air, ability to press from the front and his instinctive finishing ability.

Benjamin Sesko could raise his level under a manager who routinely improves forwards

Academy sources feel the teenager, who arrived for an initial £4million, has been unfairly criticised so far as he tries to adapt to a new club since moving up from Tottenham.

Thompson has picked up in recent academy games but in terms of his profile he looks more comfortable as a touchline winger, minus the blistering pace we usually see in that position.

His best bet is to remain in the academy and look towards a season-long loan next season.

One of the most intriguing academy prospects now that JJ Gabriel is closing in on a move to Real Madrid.

Ajayi looks physically capable of holding his own in first-team sessions and before a ball was kicked this term the development plan was to have him make a first-team debut before the season was out.

On-pitch failings may kick that can down the road but Ajayi is comfortable anywhere across the front line, has an acceleration that's invaluable and a technical level beyond his years.

Pochettino needs to take him under his wing to see what he can squeeze out of him before next summer.

VERDICT: Integrate into first-team training

#1416. Toffees Make It Five Unbeaten With Spurs Stalemate

Everton made it five games unbeaten with a hard-fought goalless draw away at high-flying Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday afternoon.

The result sees the Blues continue their strong form having thrashed Durham 6-0 on Wednesday following two stalemates against Chelsea and Manchester United in the WSL.

Ruby Mace grabbed the Player of the Match award in the capital – the midfielder repeating her award-winning performance at the home of the North Londoners last term.

It was the visitors who created the first real opportunity inside 17 minutes as Ornella Vignola teed the in-form Yuka Momiki on the edge of the area. The forward, who netted a hat-trick in the 6-0 win in midweek, looked to curl past Lize Kop, but saw her placed effort saved by the diving keeper.

History repeated itself only ten minutes later as Momiki saw another strike palmed away by the keeper. The 30-year-old drifted inside from the right and let fly upon reaching the edge of the box. Unfortunately, Kop anticipated the shot and collected after initially spilling the ball.

The hosts responded on 39 minutes as Courtney Brosnan was called in to action to deny Julie Blakstad. After breaching the Blues’ box, the Norwegian feinted before unleashing a rising strike at goal. Brosnan leapt up to tip the ball over the upright, though.

That concluded the action for a tight, physical opening 45; with Blakstad coming close once more five minutes after the interval.

Found at the back-post, the winger fired at goal and seemed destined to get on the scoresheet. However, Hannah Blundell burst forward to narrow the angle and bravely block, evading the danger.

At the other end, Everton caught Spurs on the break after Momiki held the ball up well on the halfway line. Clare Wheeler threaded it through to the advancing Vignola, who raced at goal with the ball at her feet. She pulled the trigger when faced one-on-one with Kop, but saw her low-strike sail agonisingly wide of the far-post.

Brosnan produced another fine stop five minutes later, the keeper denying Cathinka Tandenberg on this occasion. The Norway-international got down low in an attempt to nestle the ball in to the bottom right corner. Somehow, Brosnan reacted rapidly to palm it away for a corner.

Moments later, Blakstad threatened again – the forward rattling the upright on this occasion. She cut-in past Rosa van Gool and let fly, the ball striking the frame of the goal on its way out.

Head coach Scott Phelan made his first change of the game with 12 minutes remaining as Noemie Mouchon, who scored a brace against Durham on Wednesday, replaced Momiki.

The striker almost had an instant impact as she forced Kop in to a smart save. Rion Ishikawa did brilliantly down the unfamiliar right to dance past two challenges before chipping it through to the substitute. Mouchon came inside before unleashing a curling effort that was caught well by the retreating Kop.

The France-youth international came even closer in the dying minutes as she had a chance similar to Vignola previously. Like her teammate, Mouchon’s strike whistled just wide of the far-post from the right-hand side of the box.

The referee then concluded the affair, with attention now turning to Everton’s Players Cup tie with Manchester United on Wednesday night (7pm KO).
