#1319. New CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The Cas9 protein (blue; artist’s illustration) together with RNA and DNA (orange). A new therapy uses the CRISPR–Cas9 gene-editing system to treat a rare genetic disorder called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/SPL

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic condition that can cause episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR–Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, a type of hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary-angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle-cell disease and β-thalassaemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send the cells off for gene editing before infusing them back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR–Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two of Intellia’s in vivo trials for a different disorder. The agency did so after a participant with additional health conditions developed signs of liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after extra safety measures were added.

Published: 04:29 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 04:50 EST, 16 November 2026

Former Man United boss Michael Carrick was seen enjoying some time out of the spotlight as he watched The Courteeners at a gig in London over the weekend.

Carrick, 45, was relieved of his duties as United boss on Thursday following a dismal start to the season that has seen his former side pick up just eight points and one victory in ten matches.

That came despite his incredible impact in the second half of last season when he replaced Ruben Amorim and led the Red Devils to third place in the Premier League.

And on Saturday night, a few days after his tenure ended, Carrick attended a tour date of The Courteeners.

According to the band's schedule, they were performing at Alexandra Palace in London.

One fan shared a photo on X from the gig, with the caption 'One hell of a day out'.

Michael Carrick was spotted watching The Courteneers at a gig in London over the weekend

In the shot, Carrick looked relaxed and was smiling as he tried to make the most of a rare Saturday off.

The Courteeners were formed in Manchester and their frontman Liam Fray is known to be a lifelong United fan.

He regularly shared praise for Carrick during his time in the Old Trafford dugout, including backing him to get the best out of Marcus Rashford on his return to the club after his loan spell at Barcelona.

Some of The Courteeners' most famous songs include Are You In Love With A Notion? and Not Nineteen Forever, ironically the position United were in under Carrick until their 96th-minute equaliser against Aston Villa before the international break took them up to 18th place.

Following his sacking on Thursday after ten months in charge, Carrick issued a heartfelt statement reflecting on his tenure.

Posting on social media, he said: ‘I’ve had the immense privilege of leading Manchester United, the football club that I love.

‘There are very few who get to live that and feel it, and for that I’m incredibly grateful. I want to say a big thank-you to the supporters. I must say, you are a special, rare breed.

‘I know we’ve not had the results lately, but you’ve shown me nothing but love and support in times when the easiest thing, and what most end up doing, would be to turn the other way.

‘That’s what makes you who you are. That’s why I fell in love with this club all those years ago.’

Carrick was relieved of his duties at Man United on Thursday after a dismal start to the season

The axe ultimately fell on Carrick on Thursday, yet the writing was on the wall for several days beforehand as speculation spread and United's hierarchy worked towards an agreement with Mauricio Pochettino.

Many former United stars were hugely critical of their former club, with Gary Neville calling their treatment of Carrick 'disgusting', while Peter Schmeichel labelled it 'very disrespectful'.

Rio Ferdinand also compared United's 142-word statement announcing his sacking to 'like ChatGPT' after there was no comment added by club chiefs.

United are back in action on Sunday when they travel to Anfield to take on Liverpool in what will be Pochettino's first game in charge.

#1317. 20 Greatest Scottish Players in Football History [Ranked]

For a proud nation of just five and a half million, Scotland has a remarkable record of producing footballers who have gone on to make their mark at the very highest level of the game.

They are also a country with an incredible history too. Along with the "Auld Enemy" England, Scotland are the joint oldest national team in the world, due to their participation in the world's first international football match when facing the Three Lions at Hamilton Crescent on the 30th of November 1872, a fixture that in commemoration of the occasion took place every year until 1989.

Scotland's two most famous club sides, the Old Firm, Rangers and Celtic, are steeped in history too. In terms of titles, Rangers are the second most successful club in the world and were also the first British team to reach a European final, falling short to Fiorentina in the 1961 Cup Winners' Cup Final. As for Celtic, they went one step further in the 1966/67 season under legendary manager Jock Stein, becoming the first British side to win the European Cup, defeating Inter Milan in the final.

But what about some of the sport's best players? Those to have donned the dark blue shirt with the most distinction. With that in mind, here are the 20 best Scottish footballers in history.

20 Greatest Scottish Players in Football History (20-12)

Despite standing at just 5'7", footballers don't come much more intimidating than Dave Mackay. Nicknamed Football's Braveheart, Mackay had the career that he dreamed of as a boyhood Heart of Midlothian supporter, ending the club's 48-year wait for a major honour by winning an incredible seven trophies over nine seasons, including a record-breaking Scottish league championship in 1957/58.

Mackay then moved to Tottenham Hotspur and quickly established himself as an integral member of the side that saw success in the early 1960s. Indeed, many have referred to Mackay as “the heartbeat” of Spurs’ double-winning season in 1961.

The tenacious midfielder won the English top division for a second time in 1969, this time with Derby County, with his performances that season seeing him named Football Writers Association’s Player of the Year. His success with the Rams continued, as he led the club to the title in 1975, this time as manager. His achievements in both his playing and coaching career saw Mackay inducted into both the English and Scottish Hall of Fame.

The only name in the top 10 from the 21st century, Andrew Robertson, has asserted himself as one of the finest players in his position of the Premier League era. Robertson first made a name for himself at Dundee United, putting in a string of impressive performances that saw him named PFA Scotland Young Player of the Year and rewarded with his first senior Scotland cap, whilst still just a teenager.

In 2017, Robertson followed in the footsteps of several Scottish football icons in joining Liverpool and soon became an irreplaceable part of Jurgen Klopp’s team, reaching the Champions League in his first season, a competition they won the following campaign. In 2019/20, after coming close the previous year, Robertson won the Premier League, and in 2021/22 he was part of the team that won the FA Cup and Carabao Cup. Now 32, Robertson has served as captain of the Scotland National Team since 2018, becoming the nation's most capped player in 2026.

The 15 best left-backs in the history of the Premier League have been ranked in order.

John Grieg is one of football’s true one-club men. A fellow left-back, Greig joined Rangers at 17, and went on to make a staggering 755 official appearances for the club across his 17-year senior playing career. During his time at Ibrox, Grieg helped end an unwanted 35-year record of losing finals to Old Firm foe Celtic, when Rangers triumphed 3-0 in the replay of the 1963 Scottish Cup final. This was one of six Scottish Cups that Greig, along with an impressive five League Championships.

In his role as captain, Grieg was a leading figure in the club’s recovery following the Ibrox disaster in 1971. The following year, Greig captained the club to their first European silverware as the Light Blues lifted the European Cup Winners’ Cup with a 3-2 win over Dynamo Moscow in Barcelona. Greig captained his country on 15 occasions, most notably in Scotland’s famous 3-2 win in 1967 over England at Wembley, their first since winning the World Cup the previous year. At the turn of the millennium, Greig was named “The Greatest Ever Ranger” and now serves as a life president of the club.

What Grieg is to Rangers, Billy McNeill is to Celtic. Nicknamed ‘Cesar’, McNeill was the lynchpin and captain of Jock Stein’s famous Celtic team that won nine consecutive Scottish League Championships, as well as seven Scottish Cups and six League Cups in that period.

McNeill’s crowning moment, however, came in May 1967, when he captained Celtic to the European Cup with a 2-1 victory over Inter Milan at the Estadio Nacional in Lisbon. This feat saw Celtic become the first British team to win the competition, and in turn gave McNeill the honour of being the first British man to lift the European Cup.

The defender ended his playing career with a club-record 822 appearances over an illustrious 18-year playing career. McNeill went on to enjoy an impressive managerial career too, first with Aberdeen, where he was succeeded by a certain Alex Ferguson, before returning to Celtic to take over from the great Stein. Peter Swales (Chairman of Man City in 1989), said of the icon:

"If ever a man was made for a specific club, it was Billy McNeill and Glasgow Celtic. His heart was always at Parkhead."

Another star of the famous ‘Lisbon Lions’ side, the name given to the 1967 European Cup-winning Celtic team, is Jimmy Johnson. Standing at just 5’4”, Johnson was famed for incredible speed and low centre of gravity which allowed him to weave his way beyond opponents, giving him his nickname, ‘Jinky’. Once he was off, he was impossible to stop.

Like McNeill, Johnson was part of Stein’s team that won nine consecutive league championships. It was in 1967, the year of their European Cup success, that Johnson came third in the voting for the Ballon d’Or. The tricky winger scored 129 goals for The Hoops and in 2002 was named the club’s greatest ever player.

Having started his career with Partick Thistle, Alan Hansen enjoyed incredible success after making the £100,000 move to Liverpool in 1977. The Scotsman established himself as one of Liverpool's greatest ever players in an incredible 14-year spell. The ball-playing centre-back represented the Reds on 620 occasions, playing an integral role for a side that dominated English football in the 1980s. He won 25 trophies with the club, including eight league titles and three European Cups.

While he had great success at club level, his international career wasn't as fruitful. He played just 26 games for his country, with the formidable partnership of Miller and McLeish often preferred. Despite his lack of impact on an international stage, he is still regarded as one of the greatest centre-backs in football history and one of the finest players Scotland have ever produced.

One of the only players on this list to have played exclusively outside of Scotland, Billy Bremner is a member of both the English and Scottish Hall of Fame, and it’s easy to understand why. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest midfielders of his generation and was central to Leeds United’s most successful period, captaining the club to English First Division titles in 1968/69 and 1973/74, as well as winning the League Cup in 1968 and the FA Cup in 1972.

Bremner is second in the West Yorkshire club’s all-time appearance makers, with 772 over 16 years, and having played just one match fewer than the legendary Jack Charlton. In 1970, Bremner was named the FWA Football of the Year and was voted Leeds United’s greatest player of all time. The combative midfielder also earned over 50 caps for Scotland and was captain during their 1974 World Cup campaign.

Better known to younger audiences for his stern critique of the modern game on punditry panels, Graeme Souness was an equally fiery footballer during his playing days, although one of the best of his generation.

Known for his tough tackling and leadership, Souness was at the heart of the incredible success Liverpool experienced under Bob Paisley. During his time on Merseyside, Souness won an unprecedented five league titles in six seasons, as well as the European Cup just four months after joining the club. The midfielder won a further two European Cups in 1980/81 and 1983/84 before departing for Serie A with Sampdoria, winning the Coppa Italia in his first season.

Undoubtedly one of the most naturally gifted footballers Scotland has ever produced, Jim Baxter, at his peak was a joy to behold. Glasgow-born, Baxter joined Rangers in 1960, where he remained for five seasons, displaying his quality and importance to the team that won the Scottish League First Division three times, the Scottish Cup three times, and the Scottish League Cup on four occasions. In 1965, in what was his final year before departing for England, Baxter, nicknamed ‘Slim Jim’ for his agility and effortless play, came 13th in the voting for the Ballon d’Or. Sir Alex Ferguson even said of Baxter:

"Arguably the best player to play in Scottish football. He had touch, balance, vision and just this wonderful aura."

In Scotland’s infamous 3-2 win against England in 1967, Baxter starred, tormenting the then-World Champions with keepie-uppies whilst waiting for teammates to find space. Injuries and addiction saw his career curtailed and by 1970, aged just 31, Baxter announced his retirement.

One of the great strikers in the sport’s history, Denis Law twice broke the British transfer record, first with his move from his academy side Huddersfield Town to Manchester City, and then again in 1962 when he returned to England from Torino to join Manchester United. It was at United where Law enjoyed the best years of his career, forming of the greatest attacking trios in English football history alongside George Best and Bobby Charlton, and winning the First Division in 1965 and 1967.

Law spent 11 years at Old Trafford, finding the net on 237 occasions, a total that makes him the third-highest goal scorer in Manchester United's history. Moreover, Law holds the club record for the most goals scored in a single season with 43, and with 30 goals is also Scotland’s joint-highest scorer in their history.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Denis Law remains to this day the only Scottish player to have ever won the Ballon d’Or, doing so in 1964.

#1315. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

#1314. England deliver the spectacular as Three Lions strip world champions Spain of their invincibility and give Thomas Tuchel the proof that his coaching IS working, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 17:02 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 04:59 EST, 16 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel had said he wanted evidence. He needed to believe his coaching was working. He needed to see something that told him he could help England overcome those DNA deficiencies he had identified in the aftermath of the devastating World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina.

He needed a glimpse of his England team closing the gap to the best. He needed to cling on to the idea that they could overhaul Spain, that the work he was doing could improve England so much they could win the European Championship in 2028 and end this country’s cursed cycle of despair.

Proof of concept, he called it on Saturday night when England arrived in Madrid. ‘This will be proof of concept on the highest level,’ Tuchel predicted. ‘It's the biggest test in world football. Spain seems unbeatable but we are trying to take it away from them. We are up for something spectacular.’

Something spectacular is what Tuchel promised and something spectacular is what both he and England delivered. Spain had not lost for 43 matches, a world record, but number 44 was beyond them. For just over an hour, England destroyed them. They outplayed them. They stripped them of their invincibility.

And then, when Elliot Anderson was sent off after 63 minutes for pulling back Lamine Yamal, and Spain stormed back into the game, England somehow managed to hold on for a momentous victory in the screaming, yelling cauldron of the Metropolitano. This was proof alright. This was proof positive.

Sure, it was nervy for half an hour. And, yes, England nearly found a way to throw it away. But the way they played when it was 11 v 11 was enough for any England fan to believe that England under Tuchel can climb back to the summit of a major tournament and gaze down on a view they have not seen for 60 years.

England recorded a famous victory over Spain in Madrid as they won a five-goal thriller

Elliot Anderson's red card opened the door for the world champions to mount a comeback

James Trafford made a superb double save in stoppage time to preserve England's lead

Yes, this was a Nations League dead rubber because both teams were already guaranteed progress to the quarter-finals next March, but there was no mistaking its wider significance. This was proof England are good enough to turn away from the trail of tears that has been their path for so long. Before the game, Spain had held the World Cup aloft again as one final reminder of England’s failure but by the end, by the time goalkeeper James Trafford had added to the drama with a miraculous double save, the glory and the 3-2 triumph was England’s.

Spain had won their last 12 matches in succession and the sport’s last two major tournament. They had not been beaten since March 2024 and had not lost at home since September 2022. England ended that run with 10 men. What a night. It was a special kind of crazy.

England had celebrated Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph and caps record at Wembley last week but Spain took things a stage further before the game. The boys who won the U15 World Cup were introduced to the crowd. Then the World Cup itself was carried on for goalkeeper Unai Simon to hold aloft.

England ignored it all. They started the game like an express train. They nearly took the lead inside the first two minutes when Jude Bellingham met a corner from Declan Rice on the edge of the six-yard-box and was only denied by a brilliant reaction save from Simon. Gordon’s follow-up was destined for the bottom corner before it was blocked by a Spain defender.

Spain were rattled. The crowd whistled. England forced their opponents into mistake after mistake at the back. From one of those successful presses, Kane drilled a shot inches wide. Gordon, who has made such a fine start to his Barcelona career, revelled on the stage and caused right back Marc Pubill all manner of anxieties.

Spain could barely break out of their own half but when they did, after a quarter of an hour, Yamal ran at Lewis Hall and nutmegged him before Rice chopped the teenager down. Rice was booked by French referee Clement Turpin and Lamal windmilled his hands in the air to wind up the crowd.

Pubill was replaced midway through the half. It looked like an injury but it could have been hurt pride or twisted blood. Gordon had barely given him a moment’s rest. In fact, Gordon was tireless. He harried Martin Zubimendi off the ball with ease and almost set up a chance for Bellingham.

England got the goal they deserved a minute before half-time. The build-up was controversial. Anderson played a fine through ball to Kane that doubled as a crunching tackle on Marc Cucurella. Cucurella went down as if he had been shot, which is what Cucurella always does.

Ben White slotted the ball through the keeper's legs after a brilliant England move

Harry Kane celebrates goal No 93 for England after giving them the lead from the penalty spot

The referee allowed play to continue. Kane advanced on goal and turned inside Pau Cubarsi, Spain’s brilliant young defender. Cubarsi brought him down and the referee pointed to the spot. Cucurella still lay prone. Bellingham, his Real Madrid teammate, leaned over him and told him what he thought of him.

There were a whole host of VAR checks but England passed all of them. The crowd whistled their distaste. Kane missed a penalty in the Wembley game between these two teams in September but he did not miss this one. Simon guessed the right way but Kane hit it too fiercely and it bulged the back of the net. It was his 93rd goal for England.

Spain are not used to being bossed around like this. Tempers flared after the whistle blew for half-time. Ben White and Fabian Ruiz joined in a disagreement of some sort and soon there was a flurry of pushing and shoving. It stopped short of being a melee but it was obvious Spain were shaken.

Eight minutes into the second half, England went further ahead. Rice swung a corner into the centre of the box and, as the usual wrestling match unfolded, Ezri Konsa ran in gloriously unmarked and nodded the ball down and past the helpless Simon from close range.

Four minutes later, against a general backdrop of disbelief, England were three ahead. What a goal it was, too. Bellingham, who had been his usual superhuman self, muscled his way free in the centre and fed the ball out to Kane.

Kane held the ball up and played it back to Bellingham on the edge of the box. Bellingham spotted the overlapping run of White and found him with a clever pass. White took a touch and slotted the ball past Simon. It was the Arsenal full-back’s first competitive England start, too. Maybe now England fans will stop booing him.

This was the night Thomas Tuchel had been crying out for as he got the evidence he demanded

Ezri Konsa met Declan Rice's set-piece to plant an unstoppable header in the back of the net

But then, midway through the half, England gave Spain a lifeline. Jarell Quansah was caught in possession by Yamal and as Yamal bore down on goal, Anderson pulled him back. Anderson was shown a red card and Spain were awarded a penalty. Oyarzabal waited for Trafford to commit himself and then stroked the ball into the opposite corner.

The atmosphere in the stadium was transformed. Spain sensed vulnerability in England for the first time. Fifteen minutes from time, they pulled another goal back. Yamal sprinted away down the right and slid the ball into the middle for substitute Nico Williams, who sidefooted it past Trafford.

Now, it was like the Alamo. Yamal tormented England. Trafford dived at full length to push away one of his shots and then got down at his near post to divert a shot that was creeping in. White produced another of the moments of the night with a flying block to keep out a goalbound shot from Williams.

Spain threw everything at England but England would not yield. When Trafford made that double save, everyone knew. It was to be England’s night. Tuchel had his proof of concept.

#1313. Why the USA Withdrew From the U17 World Cup in Qatar & Who Replaced Them

US Soccer's decision to withdraw its team from the U17 World Cup in Qatar has brought unwanted scrutiny to the tournament. The announcement was made last Wednesday, with just over a week remaining before the opening fixtures kick off.

The American squad secured their place in the tournament earlier in 2026, ensuring they would be making a record 20th appearance at the tournament. The team qualified top of their group with a 1-1 draw in their final game against the Dominican Republic. Philadelphia Union striker Malik Jakupovic starred in qualifying, scoring eight goals — including the final, decisive goal against the Dominican Republic.

But on the verge of another major campaign, and following on from the United States' co-hosting of the 2026 World Cup, the U17 squad's efforts have now seemingly been for nothing, with US Soccer making the difficult decision to pull the plug on their participation. Now leaving a glaring hole in Group J, questions have not only been asked of US Soccer but the tournament's hosts as to why the US team have withdrawn. GIVEMESPORT have provided all the details behind the late exit and who will be replacing the United States at the tournament.

It was a decision that was made with much consideration, especially with the disappointment that would be felt by the impressive U17 squad. But US Soccer's formal notification to FIFA of its intent to withdraw went beyond reasons related to the sport and the competition itself.

US Soccer has cited escalating security concerns in the Middle East as the reason behind the decision to withdraw its team. The US Department of State issued a Level Three travel advisory for Qatar last month, advising Americans traveling to the country to reconsider due to the risk of armed conflict. Further instability in the region, including missile strikes in neighboring Saudi Arabia, also influenced the travel advisory.

In a letter sent to players and coaching staff and seen by news agency Reuters, US Soccer stated that hostile behavior in the region has "the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."

"The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority," US Soccer emphasized in the letter.

Whilst still a shock to the international football community, tournament withdrawals are not unheard of. Coincidentally, North Korea's U17 team withdrew from the U17 Asian Cup earlier this year. In 1950, India, Scotland, and Turkey — who had all qualified for that year's World Cup — all withdrew for various reasons.

Scotland infamously withdrew after stating that they would only travel to the tournament in Brazil if they qualified as British Home Champions. After finishing second in the British Home Championship behind England, the SFA held their stance and refused to send the team despite qualifying for the World Cup. India and Turkey both cited financial constraints as their reasons behind their withdrawal from the same tournament.

The World Cup is set to be bigger than ever next year but a handful of nations still missed out on the chance to qualify.

They were frustrated by the United States in their final qualifying fixture, but the US team's loss is the Dominican Republic's gain.

The Caribbean island finished second in Group E of the 2026 CONCACAF U17 World Cup qualification stage, missing out on goal difference alone. Their inability to find a way past the stubborn US defence, playing out a 1-1 draw in the decisive final group game, meant that the Dominican Republic went agonisingly close to qualifying.

But with the US team's withdrawal, the Caribbean nation will now make its history-making debut at the U17 World Cup. Under FIFA competition regulations, the governing body holds the right to appoint a replacement team when a qualified nation withdraws. The Dominican Republic earned the spot due to its strong showing during the qualifiers.

As well as holding the US to a 1-1 draw, the Dominican Republic prolifically defeated the other two teams in Group E. A 10-0 win over the Grenadines and a 5-0 win over Saint Kitts and Nevis marked the country out as one of the best performing teams that failed to qualify.

The U17 squad will now head to Qatar to join Group J, where they will battle it out against Algeria, Chile, and Montenegro for a place in the knockout phase. And the team have a number of standout players who will be looking to make a name for themselves on the international stage.

Striker Adrian Garcia Jaquez scored a number of crucial goals in qualifying, including the equaliser against the US. He is a part of La Liga 2 side Leganes' youth setup. There's also centre back Alejandro Lopez, who spent seven years in the Atletico Madrid academy before moving to Rayo Vallecano. He earned his first senior cap for the Dominican Republic earlier this year. Goalkeeper Aidan Betances has also been impressive, conceding just one goal in qualifying. He is currently a part of the New York Red Bulls academy.

US Soccer have withdrawn its Under-17 men's national team from the upcoming FIFA World Cup in Qatar.

#1312. Report Napoli reject PSV bid for De Bruyne

Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf reports that Napoli have rejected an opening bid from PSV Eindhoven for Kevin De Bruyne worth €2m.

Napoli have reportedly rejected an opening offer for their midfielder De Bruyne.

According to De Telegraaf, the Partenopei have turned down a €2m bid from Dutch side PSV, who have already opened talks with the ex-Manchester City star.

De Bruyne’s contract at the Stadio Maradona expires at the end of the season, and the midfielder has recently refused to rule out a possible January switch to PSV.

According to the report, De Bruyne is open to moving to PSV in the January window, which would allow him and his family to move into the home they own in the Belgian Limburg.

It is still unclear whether Napoli will be open to selling the experienced midfielder in January.

According to De Telegraaf, the Partenopei will ask for a higher transfer fee, while Corriere dello Sport claims the Serie A side wants to retain De Bruyne until the end of the season.

Napoli hold an option to extend De Bruyne’s contract until 2028, while Gazzetta reports that Frank Zambo-Anguissa, rather than the Belgian, could leave in January, with Marseille interested in the Cameroonian midfielder.

#1311. Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) and lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) across Brazil have traces of microplastics circulating in their blood — even if they live more than 60 kilometres away from human infrastructure. Researchers found that these animals carry roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood on average — similar to the levels of plastics found in humans — with the highest levels found in those that lived closest to urban areas and waste-management facilities. The findings are an important step to better understand how these particles impact wildlife, says geochemist Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou.

Artificial-intelligence giant Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an upgrade to their AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences. The tool, announced on 11 November, has already impressed researchers. Its underlying AI model was trained on gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million individual cells, across 68 tissues. But the tool can also make predictions when fed data from cell types that it wasn’t trained on, which could help researchers more quickly identify variants underlying disease, says DeepMind scientist Adam Gayoso.

An approach that measures waist circumference and focuses on excess body fat could be a more accurate way to diagnose obesity — and identify people with related health risks — than body mass index (BMI). In an analysis of data from more than 800,000 people, researchers found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The new framework classified an extra 5–9% of people as having obesity, who would have been labelled only as overweight with the BMI-based approach.

Bioengineered bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form for plants could replace up to half of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, slashing the greenhouse-gas emissions associated with these chemicals, researchers suggest. Bacteria can deliver nitrogen to roots more efficiently than synthetic fertilizers, and scientists are engineering them to feed nitrogen to crop plants that don’t have natural microbial partners, such as maize and wheat. Gene-edited biofertilizers have already been used in the United States, but a slew of advances are needed to demonstrate higher levels of nitrogen fixation.

In July, artificial-intelligence titan Anthropic acquired a biotechnology company that developed two promising drug leads with just one full-time human employee and an AI assistant. The mini-firm benefited from the help of several part-time consultants and external research organizations to craft its products — two early-stage antibodies designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy — and many more researchers will be required to take the drugs forward. But the acquisition has sparked discussion about whether one-person, AI-enabled biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future.

With the rise of multidisciplinary science and artificial intelligence, biologists are “poised to at last understand the complexity of life”, writes epigeneticist Edith Heard, chief executive of the Francis Crick Institute, London. But people are what will unlock these discoveries, not technology alone. “Funders, institutions and scientific leaders must embrace new technologies while protecting the conditions in which discovery thrives: curiosity, collaboration and, above all, the freedom and support to follow unexpected observations to see where they lead,” Heard writes.

“Environmental change is altering the conditions in which brains develop and minds are sustained”, says a new report from a commission convened by Nature Mental Health. For example, heat, air and noise pollution and loss of green space have been linked with depression, anxiety and cognitive decline — with poorer people, children and older people among those most exposed. The Earth–Brain–Health Commission offers a new framework for uniting neuroscience, psychiatry, public health and environmental science around shared challenges and solutions.

Nature Mental Health editorial | 6 min read

Get the gist in the accompanying policy brief (9 min read)

Reference: Nature Mental Health Earth–Brain–Health Commission report

The lawless simulated world of blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) — which is just about to release its sixth iteration — offers researchers an intricately crafted testbed for road-safety experiments, says computer scientist Julius Schöning. (BBC | 7 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03684-x

Today I’m adding M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything to my reading list. The post-apocalyptic novel was announced as the winner of this year’s Booker prize on 9 November — the first “bona fide” science-fiction novel to win the award, says Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation.

Let me know what other science-fiction books I should add to the pile, along with your feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

#1310. Kean: Como and Italy striker’s return from injury delayed

Multiple sources in Italy say Moise Kean’s return to action with Como has been delayed due to a new tibia issue.

Italy and Como striker Kean will be out longer than expected.

The 26-year-old last played in October, featuring in Italy’s 1-1 draw against France, and was expected to miss five weeks.

However, La Provincia di Como and Sky Sport Italia claim that Kean will need more time to recover.

According to La Provincia di Como, Kean recently saw a new specialist, while Sky claims the striker has developed new problems in his tibia.

Sky confirms Kean’s recent specialist visit, adding that it took place in Barcelona in the past few days.

Although the nature of his new problem remains unclear, Kean won’t be back anytime soon, as both media outlets say the ex-Fiorentina and Juventus star needs more time to return to action.

Kean joined Como from Fiorentina in a €40m deal last summer. The Italy international scored one goal and provided one assist in six appearances before his injury.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1309. Ashley Cole accidentally shooting a student, bare-chested Marcus Bent threatening police with a meat cleaver - and an ex-Barcelona star firing a gun in a hospital! Footballers' fascination with weapons after Amar Dedic's bow and arrows saga

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and WILL GOVE

Published: 07:00 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 05:44 EST, 16 November 2026

Amar Dedic might have fancied himself as Robin Hood – but the Newcastle United defender's latest adventure in the Northumberland countryside led to a rather less merry altercation with police last week.

The Magpies star sparked a major police operation after being spotted carrying a bow and arrows near a reservoir outside Newcastle, with at least six patrol cars joining the search for the £30million player.

After tracking down and questioning the Bosnian, officers were satisfied there was no threat to the public and that the equipment was intended for recreational use.

But Dedic's escapade was certainly not the first time a footballer has found himself in hot water over the possession, carrying or use of a weapon, with brass knuckles, meat cleavers and BB guns among the bizarre arsenal of items to have attracted the authorities' attention over the years.

Marcus Bent, with a meat cleaver, in Surrey

Former Middlesbrough and Everton forward Marcus Bent was tasered in his own home by police after threatening armed police officers with a meat cleaver and kitchen knife while under the influence of cocaine.

Bent, who avoided jail in 2016 after he pleaded guilty to possession of cocaine and affray, called Surrey Police after thinking he had discovered an intruder in his home.

Officers arrived at the scene but were initially unable to gain access to the property. Guildford Crown Court heard how the officers were about to use a battering ram to gain entry when a bare-chested Bent 'flung' open the door holding two chef's knives, with his 'eyes wide, jaw clenched and his body rigid'.

Bent, who was handed a 12-month sentence, suspended for two years, later said: 'I was paranoid and I was hallucinating. I felt there were people in my house. I remember thinking the door handle was moving.

'At no point was I ever going to take someone's life. I called them because I was hallucinating, paranoid, terrified.'

Marcus Bent arrives at court before pleading guilty to possession of cocaine and affray

Ashley Cole, with an air rifle, in Cobham

To most, Ashley Cole is England's all-time greatest full-back but the three-time Premier League winner also made headlines for an infamous training ground air rifle incident.

Back in 2011 while playing for Chelsea, Ashley Cole accidentally shot and injured 21-year-old student Tom Cowan, who was on work experience at the Blues' training ground in Cobham, Surrey.

The Champions League winning left-back was reportedly 'larking about' with a .22 air rifle and accidentally shot Cowan from just five feet away.

The student had assumed he would get an invaluable experience on his brief visit to Cobham but instead had to be treated by medics and rest for the remainder of the day after the shot was fired.

Cole accidentally shot a 21-year-old on work experience at Chelsea's training ground

Ex-England star Darren Bent ran into trouble early in his career when he was questioned over the alleged shooting of a 12-year-old boy with a ball-bearing gun.

While starring for his boyhood club Ipswich at the age of 20 in May 2004, Bent was arrested on suspicion of possession of an imitation firearm with intent to cause violence, before he was placed on bail and eventually released without charge pending further investigations.

According to a Suffolk Police statement at the time, a 12-year-old boy at a play area in Kesgrave had been struck in the back by a pellet from a ball-bearing gun (BB Gun). The incident was reported to authorities by his mother.

Bent, who was given a formal caution for his actions, went on to enjoy a fruitful career in the Premier League, representing the likes of Charlton, Tottenham, Sunderland and Aston Villa while also winning 13 caps for the Three Lions.

Early on his career Premier League legend Darren Bent was arrested on suspicion of possession of an imitation firearm

Karim Adeyemi, with brass knuckles, in Germany

The only member of this list to still be playing is Germany and Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi who was fined £396,000 in 2025 for possessing a pair of brass knuckles.

The former Borussia Dortmund forward was caught with the knuckles back in 2024, at the age of 22, but had to wait until the following year to receive his punishment.

Under German law the possession, procurement and use of brass knuckles is prohibited. The young winger avoided a public trial and a criminal record and was given a fine consisting of 60 daily payments of £6,600.

Although he never used the weapon, the German was in hot water  as he briefly lost his starting place in the German national team and at Borussia Dortmund.

The Westphalia giants released a statement saying: 'BVB always takes criminal allegations seriously and uses them as an opportunity to discuss them with its employees while respecting confidentiality obligations.'

Adeyemi was lucky to dodge prison time after being charged with the possession of brass knuckles

Diego Maradona, with an air rifle, in Buenos Aires

Argentina icon Diego Maradona caused injuries to four people when he fired an air rifle at journalists and photographers while hiding behind a parked Mercedes outside his Buenos Aires home in February 1994.

Four years later, Maradona was found guilty of assault with a weapon and given a suspended prison sentence of two years and ten months, which was later reduced to an even two years.

To many he is the best of all time but Diego Maradona is hardly infallible off the pitch

Despite appealing against the sentence which they claimed was 'too light', the journalists injured by Maradona said the verdict at least demonstrated there was 'justice for all' in Argentina.

'At least this exemplary case does show that there is justice for all,' said Daniel Talamoni, one of the four reporters who sued the World Cup winner.

'When the case began four years ago, everyone said it was impossible. They would sentence a man idolised in Argentina and forgive everything.'

Arda Turan, with an unlicensed gun, in a Turkish hospital

Keen fans of European football will not need to be reminded of who Arda Turan is. But they may be surprised to learn that the former Atletico Madrid and Barcelona star has had some serious trouble with the law.

Turan somehow avoided a jail sentence after discharging an unlicensed firearm in a hospital

In 2018 while on loan from Barcelona in his home country of Turkey at Istanbul Basaksehir, Turan got into an altercation with Turkish singer Berkay Sahin, who ended in hospital with a broken nose.

Then Turan turned up at the hospital that was treating Sahin with an unlicensed firearm, and fired a shot into the floor.

He was eventually sentenced to two years and eight months behind bars for firing a gun to cause panic, illegal possession of weapons and intentional injury but the sentence was suspended for five years. Basaksehir also fined the midfielder £350,000 over the incident.

Nearly a decade after the incident, Turan now manages Ukrainian powerhouse Shakhtar Donetsk, joining the club in May of last year.

#1308. Juventus favour Barcelona defender over Tottenham’s, but top target remains clear

Il Corriere dello Sport reports that Barcelona’s Alejandro Balde is Juventus’ top left-back target for January, but the Bianconeri are also looking to Lorenzo Bernasconi for 2027-28.

Juventus are expected to bring in some reinforcements during the January transfer window, including a new left-back.

Corriere dello Sport reports that Barcelona’s Balde is the Old Lady’s top priority in that position, with the Serie A giants hoping to sign the Spaniard on a six-month loan.

Gazzetta had already reported on Juventus’ interest in Balde, describing the Spaniard as a “dream target” for the Bianconeri.

According to CorSport, Juventus prefer Balde over Rayan Ait-Nouri (Man City), Juan Miranda (Bologna) and Destiny Udogie (Tottenham), while Bernasconi is their top target for the 2027-28 season.

Juventus already held talks with Atalanta last summer, and Bernasconi signed a contract extension with La Dea just a few hours ago; the club confirmed the new deal yesterday, Monday, November 16.

According to Corriere dello Sport, Atalanta already demanded a fee close to €30m for Bernasconi last summer, so if Juventus can’t afford him in January, they’ll try to get Balde on loan and then resume talks with La Dea at the end of the season.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1307. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

But beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area showed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

“There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

Carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”

Martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”

The Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

“We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

“It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

“It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

“We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

“It took us a little bit to adjust to it, but I don’t think it was too difficult to adjust. It was more down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.”

Brighton & Hove Albion 5 Crystal Palace 0

It’s all over at Elland Road, with Leeds and Man Utd playing out a competitive draw. Mbeumo’s opener was cancelled out by Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser in a game that was low on attacking quality and chances. Ultimately, a draw was a very fair reflection of the match. Man Utd are 14th and winless in six games across all competitions, while Leeds move into the top seven.

Lisandro Martinez keeps his place despite his rant at the Old Trafford board in midweek but the bigger concern has been his individual performances this season - they have been nowhere near good enough and he’s brought extra scrutiny on himself with the tirade. Leeds are the kind of compact, organised, aggressive in-your-face team United have tended to struggle against in recent years. They were good in defeat to Arsenal last weekend and showcased their considerable threat in the 4-1 win over Newcastle. Expect a white-hot atmosphere at Elland Road. They cannot stand Manchester United in these parts.

Lisandro Martínez delivered a strong and powerful message to his Manchester United team-mates: if you’re playing terribly, use the director of football as a punchbag and you might become a hero.

It is a popular play in a world in which certain players have become as adept at scapegoat-hunting as man-marking. Passionately speak about what someone else at your football club is doing wrong – particularly the unloved executives – and cast yourself as a whistleblower, selflessly exposing the truth that the long-suffering supporters deserve.

Such internal fights make for great drama, unless your own club is caught in the middle of it.

That’s why in the immediate aftermath of Martínez’s scathing comments about Jason Wilcox following the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid, there was a division between those who celebrated the Argentine speaking out and those who felt it was self-serving, a convenient deflection by an out-of-form player in the final year of his contract.

The narrative is completely dominated by the drama around Man Utd, which should suit Leeds perfectly. All eyes and pressure is on their opponents, and they have every reason to feel confident ahead of this huge clash at Elland Road.

Kobbie Mainoo is also sidelined, while Matheus Cunha and Marcus Rashford are benched. With Benjamin Sesko still out, Bryan Mbeumo starts up top and is likely to be supported out wide by Amad Diallo and Bruno Fernandes.

Michael Carrick also starts Carlos Baleba for the second match running, and he’s partnered in midfield by Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. Just 10 months on from Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United, the club return to Elland Road on Sunday afternoon with another manager under pressure and the director of football again in the spotlight.

The difference is Michael Carrick still has a chance to determine the course of his United future whereas Amorim had already sealed his fate after a furious bust-up with Jason Wilcox 48 hours before his last game ended in a 1-1 draw with Leeds and post-match fireworks.

But even for a club never far from a crisis, it seems remarkable to think they are back in a tailspin so soon after Amorim’s sacking in early January.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Leeds United at Elland Road.

Quiet week in the world of Man Utd? Don’t be silly. Following a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid in Spain on Wednesday, defender Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on Man Utd’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s hierarchy because of a dreadful start to the campaign, which has yielded two victories in nine games across all competitions.

The Argentine criticised Man Utd’s recruitment and said he expected more, but didn’t suggest Carrick was to blame. Martinez has since apologised for his outburst and met with Wilcox, Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada and Michael Carrick, with Telegraph Sport understanding that he’s free to play today, although his role remains unclear as we all eagerly await the team news.

Carrick is under immense pressure to get a result here in Yorkshire, with last weekend’s 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford condemning Man Utd to their worst league start for 40 years.

With all eyes on the visitors, Leeds will be licking their lips at the prospect of piling further misery on their beleaguered opponents. Daniel Farke’s side suffered their first Premier League loss last weekend, falling 2-1 to Arsenal at the Emirates after going a goal up, but the mood remains positive after a solid start to the campaign.

Leeds are eighth and the club will be harbouring ambitions of a top-half finish in the Premier League for the first time since the 2019/20 season, with the prospect of qualifying for European football not out of the realm of possibility.

Unlike Man Utd, Leeds have a settled, reliable system that clearly suits their current squad. Elland Road will also be a cauldron of hostility and noise, given the fierce backdrop between these two bitter rivals.

This has all the ingredients to be a thrilling and fascinating watch as we bring you the latest updates, information and drama. Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1306. RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Liam Drew is a freelance science journalist based near London.

Protection against the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) must expand to lower-income countries, which are harder hit.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty

“Something’s wrong with the data. There are too few people in hospitals” with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), epidemiologist Caroline Klint Johannesen recalls a colleague remarking while analysing Danish health records for last winter.

On 1 October 2025, Denmark introduced a nationwide policy of vaccinating pregnant people against RSV — a respiratory pathogen that usually causes mild symptoms but can lead to severe disease and even death in vulnerable people, including infants and older adults. Maternal antibodies induced by the vaccine cross the placenta to protect babies for around the first six months of their lives, when they are most at risk. Newborns at high risk of severe disease, including premature infants, whose mothers had not been vaccinated, were given injections of monoclonal antibodies.

RSV wave hammers hospitals — but vaccines and treatments are coming

RSV wave hammers hospitals — but vaccines and treatments are coming

Johannesen, a vaccine researcher at Nordsjællands Hospital in Hillerød, Denmark, found1 that infant hospital admissions plummeted. The immunizations are working, she says (see ‘Newborn protection’).

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that every year, RSV hospitalizes roughly 3.6 million and kills about 100,000 children under 5 years old. Of these deaths, 97% occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

The virus is also dangerous to older adults — although those risks are widely underappreciated by both physicians and the public. Historically, testing has been sparse, and there are no global statistics for RSV-related adult deaths. But over the age of 60, hospitalizations and mortality increase with age, especially in people with other diseases such as chronic heart and lung conditions. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that between around 10,000 and 25,000 people have died in each of the past two winters, especially in older age groups.

Since 2022, when European regulators approved nirsevimab — a long-acting monoclonal antibody against RSV — a second antibody and three vaccines have been developed for use in adults, one of which is suitable for pregnant people.

“It’s just remarkable,” says Buddy Creech, a paediatrician at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee, to have gone “from no mechanism to prevent RSV to an embarrassment of riches”. Dozens of countries across Europe, Asia and North and South America have launched various immunization programmes.

#1305. Youngsters will get their chance, Bruno Fernandes can thrive and touchline energy will be vital: Key lessons for Man United from incoming boss Mauricio Pochettino's 6-0 USA masterclass

Published: 18:47 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 05:54 EST, 16 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino enjoyed a stellar penultimate game in charge of the United States, thrashing Haiti 6-0.

The newly appointed Manchester United manager has just one game left before sinking his teeth into the job at Old Trafford.

He will link up with United on Wednesday, but first must navigate the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final tie with Haiti on Tuesday.

Here, Pochettino cut a fairly reserved figure on the touchline as he was rewarded for trusting youth - and even saw his team score from a corner, something United don't do much of these days.

Without further ado, here are four things Manchester United fans learned from the win.

Mauricio Pochettino, dressed in a scarf, was fairly reserved as the United States beat Haiti 6-0

Pochettino’s arrival spells good news for United’s proud tradition of promoting homegrown youth - it is glad tidings for the likes of Shea Lacey and Kobbie Mainoo. You wonder if, for a while, JJ Gabriel will look on forlornly from Real Madrid’s reserves.

The Argentinian handed out 13 debuts in the September-October international break, including to eight teenagers in one 4-1 victory over Peru.

His strategy was no different here as he started 18-year-old Julian Hall up front and Diego Kochen, 20, in goal - both players he has given debuts to this year. He was rewarded, with Hall scoring his fourth goal in just five games for the United States, while Kochen kept a clean sheet.

Despite his affinity for the stars of tomorrow, he is a hard schoolmaster. In a column for The Athletic in 2022, he revealed that he sat a young Harry Kane down for a brutal meeting where he showed him stats and clips to justify why he wasn’t playing him more.

Pochettino had known Kane’s potential from their first training session but wanted the ‘tough conversation’ to get the best out of him. Kane went on to score 169 goals under him for Tottenham, and now he’s the best player in the world.

His trust in fresh faces could inject some much-needed enthusiasm around the club, strengthen the squad's connection with the fanbase, and increase the energy levels in one of the Premier League's oldest, most lethargic teams.

The likes of Shea Lacey will be delighted at how Pochettino puts trust in younger players

Julian Hall, 18, struck his fourth goal in five games for the United States under Pochettino

Pochettino has a history of getting the most out of attacking midfielders such as Dele Alli, Christian Eriksen, and Adam Lallana. You can add Cole Palmer to that list too, though he was primarily a right winger under him at Chelsea.

Manchester United desperately need him to get a tune out of Bruno Fernandes, who has cut a frustrated figure this season and whose creative efficiency has declined - though he still has nine goal involvements.

If Christian Pulisic’s performance against Haiti is anything to go by, Fernandes will be happy. The attacking midfielder scored twice, playing a free role and being given penalty duty.

The 28-year-old was also asked to muck in defensively, and that’s something Fernandes is willing to do. Across the seasons, he has often covered more ground than any of his team-mates.

Pochettino and Pulisic have seemingly had a distant relationship, despite the latter’s insistence to the contrary. The manager branded it ‘b*******’ when the AC Milan star opted out of the Gold Cup last year, and left him out of his selection a couple of months ago, bringing in 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan.

Asked about Pochettino's upcoming final game, Pulisic said at full-time: 'We're treating it like any other game.' No emotion on display.

Depending on how you interpret Fernandes - either a die-for-the-badge club servant or a primadonna - Pochettino could draw the best or worst out of the Portuguese.

Pochettino often gets the best out of attacking midfielders - will he work well with Bruno Fernandes?

He has had a distant relationship with Christian Pulisic, but the AC Milan star scored twice here

Pochettino tends to push his defensive lines high up the pitch and his strategy with the United States has been no different.

They were almost caught out for trying to play the offside trap early on as a simple ball from midfield sent Danley Jean Jacques through one-on-one, forcing Kochen into a good save.

Meanwhile, full-backs Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman were constantly pushing high and overlapping in his 4-2-3-1 system - although you’d obviously expect a strong level of intent when they’re favourites against Haiti.

Given his high-line tradition, Pochettino may well favour more mobile defenders such as Leny Yoro and Patrick Dorgu.

The battle for Harry Maguire will be to convince his new boss that his other qualities compensate for his lack of pace.

Pochettino takes inspiration from the frenetic football of Marcelo Bielsa, who managed him at Newell’s Old Boys in Argentina.

But he'll have to balance his philosophy with the reality of United's woeful defensive record this campaign. Just the 15 goals conceded in the last five games...

Pochettino showed an eagerness to intervene early in the game - a possible boost after Michael Carrick suffered from slow starts

Pochettino is typically seen as an animated character on the touchline, in contrast to Carrick's statesmanlike behaviour, but he spent lots of time in his seat here.

He has calmed down somewhat these days - though he did kick a crate of bottles in frustration at the World Cup - and didn’t even react much when his team scored.

A major criticism of Carrick is that he takes too long to change things in-game, often going late with substitutions. Pochettino has traditionally leaned that way, too, but he was eager to influence proceedings here.

Even three minutes in, at a break while Antonee Robinson was being treated, he called Pulisic over for what looked like an intense tactical chat.

United have been plagued by slow starts this season, so it was encouraging to see Pochettino so alert and full of ideas early into the game. He could have coasted, really, but wanted to eke out every advantage.
